articles.title_orig: Trump blew past deadline to halt running taxpayer-funded campaign-style ads
articles.title_zh: Trump blew past deadline to halt running taxpayer-funded campaign-style ads
articles.content_orig:
President Trump leaves the stage after speaking during an election rally in Syracuse, New York on Oct. 9, 2026. Alex Wong/Getty Images hide caption
Ads promoting President Trump and his policies continued to be paid for by the U.S. government well after Trump announced he would have his MAGA Inc. super PAC take over funding the ads and kept airing despite a federal judge ordering them to come down.
An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer dollars has been spent to air the ads since the campaign began in late September. Nearly $10 million of that total was spent after Oct. 5, when the president pledged to fund it privately in a post on Truth Social .
"The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump posted at the time. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc."
The ads have been criticized by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle with Republicans praising the president's choice to shift funding for the ads to an outside super PAC. But, that praise was premature. Despite giving the impression that there'd been a policy change, the government-funded ads didn't stop airing after Trump's post.
The White House has repeatedly referred to the ads as public service announcements, but a lawsuit filed by Common Cause and others argued they were being funded without congressional approval and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda produced with taxpayer dollars.
The ads — five of them in all — cover a wide range of pro-Trump content. One includes a splashy montage of photos of the president with a chorus singing "love me" serving as the soundtrack. Another is an exact duplicate of an ad made by the Trump campaign during the 2024 election cycle. Two promote the military operations in Venezuela and Iran. All of them end with the words "Paid for by the U.S. Government" on the screen.
The spots continued being broadcast for several hours after a federal judge overseeing the lawsuit issued a temporary ruling Sunday night saying the government "shall cancel or cause to be cancelled any slot, placement, reservation, or arrangement for the airing or dissemination of the challenged advertisements, including those placements for the evening of October 11, 2026."
Pro-Trump spots aired hundreds of additional times Sunday night into the wee hours of Monday morning.
"The last PSAs paid for by the government aired yesterday evening," a White House official not authorized to speak publicly told NPR on Monday afternoon, adding that the government "did not receive notice from the court in time to cancel the ad buys. The PSAs will be paid for by outside groups moving forward."
The White House had previously said that taxpayer funds used for ads would not be reimbursed. The White House has also insisted these ads were merely about promoting patriotism. They argued the ads can't be campaign related because the president isn't running for office this year and have nothing to do with the midterm elections next month. But Trump has repeatedly implored voters to vote like he is on the ballot and his dismal approval ratings have been dragging down Republicans all over the country.
A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found the ads are pretty unpopular. The poll asked whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to use "taxpayer funds to pay for election-related television ads featuring the President or members of his cabinet." It wasn't even close, with 86% of Americans saying it is inappropriate. Even 80% of Republicans said the ads were inappropriate.
It's rare to get such bipartisan agreement on anything these days.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_orig: Death on Six Flags rollercoaster in US triggers ride closures across six states
articles.title_zh: Death on Six Flags rollercoaster in US triggers ride closures across six states
articles.content_orig:
Six Flags says nine rollercoasters across six amusement parks temporarily closed after reported fatal incident on Goliath ride in Georgia
Theme park company Six Flags temporarily closed nine rollercoasters across six amusement parks on Monday after one person died and several others were injured in an incident involving a coaster in Georgia .
A spokesperson for the park said they closed similar attractions across their parks “out of an abundance of caution” after the incident at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (24km) north-west of Atlanta .
Officials did not confirm how the person died, nor how the others were injured or their conditions.
Cobb County police department’s major crimes unit has launched an investigation.
Witnesses who spoke to NBC affiliate WXIA of Atlanta said they saw a man fall from the Goliath rollercoaster. “He fell and hit the car three different times,” one witness told the station.
A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they are fully cooperating with local authorities as they investigate.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said, adding that they are providing support to the guests and team members impacted.
Authorities and Six Flags did not identify the rollercoaster. However, local TV stations showed video of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster.
The rollercoaster, which was opened in 2006, reaches top speeds of 70mph (about 113 kph) and heights of 200 feet (61 meters), the park’s website reports. During about 3 1/2 minutes, riders “navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills”, according to the website.
“I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one,” Lisa Cupid, the Cobb County board of commissioners chair, said in a statement. She added that next of kin have been notified.
The amusement park is a major part of the county’s tourism and brings in visitors from across the south-east, Cupid said.
“We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories,” she said.
The incident comes less than two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain, in Southern California, announced that it is retiring its famous X2 rollercoaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride.
The park had settled one wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022.
Last year, a 32-year-old man died after riding a high-speed rollercoaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. He died from blunt impact injuries and his death was ruled accidental.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq falls ahead of earnings, economic data while oil rallies
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq falls ahead of earnings, economic data while oil rallies
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures were mixed early Tuesday, with traders digesting a slew of corporate earnings reports from major banks along with a steep overnight decline in South Korea that put pressure on memory names.
S&P 500 futures were down 0.1%, while Nasdaq-100 futures lost 0.5%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures outperformed, rising 118 points, or 0.2% — though they traded well off their session highs.
JPMorgan Chase reported a revenue miss for the third quarter, sending the stock down more than 2%. Wells Fargo also shed 2% on weaker-than-expected Q3 numbers. Citigroup and Goldman Sachs are due later on Tuesday.
UnitedHealth, meanwhile, rose 1% after the insurance giant's results exceeded analyst expectations.
Memory stocks were under pressure after South Korea's Kospi benchmark dropped 5.5% — reaching its lowest level since July 31 — on valuation concerns in the space along with growing competition out of China. This week, China's CXMT said it plans to release a new, more powerful chip by year-end.
SK hynix and Western Digital dropped around 5% each, while Micron, Seagate Technology and Sandisk all fell more than 3%.
Big banks JPMorgan , Goldman Sachs , Citigroup and Wells Fargo are slated to release their results before the open on Tuesday.
The early reports could set the tone for an earnings season with lofty expectations. Analysts on average expect S&P 500 profits grew by nearly 30% from the year-earlier period, according to FactSet.
"Three groups will likely shape how investors read the season: 1) Banks (consumer and business health), 2) Big Tech (AI monetization), and 3) Energy (the durability of oil-driven profits)," wrote Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise. "Underneath these areas, the health of consumers and businesses amid higher interest rates, elevated costs, and concerns about the macroeconomic environment will be closely monitored across sectors throughout the season."
Investors on Tuesday will also parse through existing home sales figures along with commentary from Federal Reserve officials Tom Barkin and Susan Collins.
Later in the week, inflation data for September will be released – which could jolt Treasury yields after they reached multidecade highs recently. The U.S. bond market was closed Monday due to the Indigenous Peoples' Day holiday.
Wall Street is coming off a mixed session. The Dow ended Monday more than 195 points higher, while declines in memory stocks pushed the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 into negative territory for the day.
In Europe, shares were broadly higher on Tuesday, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 gaining 0.7% in morning trading. London's FTSE 100 led gains among major regional bourses, on a rise of 0.8%.

For more, check out CNBC's live coverage of bank earnings.
The health insurance giant popped 3% on third-quarter results that beat analyst expectations. UnitedHealth earned an adjusted $4.69 per share on revenue of $112.69 billion. Analysts estimated a profit of $4.14 per share on revenue of $111.40 billion.
France's parliament begins debate on the 2027 budget Tuesday as high deficits, rising debt and student protests sharpen the political cost of fiscal consolidation.
Treasury yields moved lower as investors look ahead to key economic data releases this week, including the latest U.S. inflation print.
The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans, and credit card debt — fell more than 5 basis points to 5.1937%.
The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasurys — which tend to move on geopolitical events — was down 4 basis points at 5.5580%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note , which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, fell more than 2 basis points to 4.7658%.
Luxury goods giant LVMH was trading just below the flatline shortly after the opening bell as organic sales declined in fashion and leather goods in its third quarter amid a slowdown in demand from China.
The Louis Vuitton and Dior owner posted 57.1 billion euros ($63.9 billion) in revenue in the first nine months of 2026. The company saw weakness in its fashion and leather goods offering, with organic sales down 5% year-on-year.
The company's shares were trading just below the flatline shortly after the opening bell and are down 41% since the beginning of the year. The decline weighed on the broader luxury sector, with Kering and Richemont shares also trading lower.
The company said organic revenue growth in its third quarter reflected a "less buoyant environment in China," while the U.S., Europe and Japan saw good growth.
"The problem is fashion and leather is about 75% of the operating profit [for LVMH], so that's really what counts, and the numbers are not good, and it doesn't seem to be looking great for the other peers," AIR Capital's Head of Research Pierre-Olivier Essig said on CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe," on Tuesday.
Essig added that the brand is "lost in translation" when it comes to appealing to the younger generations.
"These Gen A, Gen Z, they're different. They're not going to wait 10 years for a bag or a watch. They want it now. They're very well informed," he said.
European luxury stocks fell in early trading after French conglomerate LVMH posted weaker-than-expected earnings after the bell on Monday.
Paris-listed shares of the company were 0.3% lower in early trading. Shares of Switzerland's Richemont were 0.8% lower, while Gucci owner Kering fell 0.4%. Burberry, Moncler and Brunello Cucinelli were all higher.
LVMH reported worse-than-expected organic sales growth in its third quarter earnings on Monday, with weak Chinese demand damaging performance in its leather and fashion brands.
"As the first luxury company to report 3Q26, LVMH's Fashion & Leather miss is unlikely to improve sentiment towards soft luxury," Citi analysts said in a Monday evening note.
Deutsche Bank's Adam Cochrane said in a note that LVMH had "managed to miss relatively weak investor expectations."
"Despite the stock trading at near an all-time low valuation … it is hard to see what could change investor sentiment in the short term," he said, but he noted that his team sees LVMH's performance as a "cyclical rather than structural problem" with "the risk/reward weighted to the upside."
European stocks opened broadly higher on Tuesday, with the pan-continental Stoxx 600 gaining 0.4% in early deal making. Banking, chemicals and utilities stocks were among the top performers, with London's FTSE 100 leading gains among regional bourses.
Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 1.82% lower at 67,777.52, while South Korea's Kospi dropped 5.46%.
Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 was flat at 8,783.90.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was down nearly 1% in its last hour of trade on Tuesday, while mainland China's CSI 300 closed 0.29% lower at 4,275.68.
European chip stocks sank in early morning trade, with semiconductor equipment maker ASML down 3.3%, and STMicroelectronics and German chip maker Infineon both down 5%. Dutch firms BE Semiconductor and ASM International were both around 4% lower at the open.
Oil giant BP said Tuesday that its third-quarter results are expected to include post-tax adjusting items relating to impairment charges in the range of $3 billion to $4.5 billion.
"These charges are primarily attributable to transition businesses in the gas & low carbon energy segment and are excluded from underlying replacement cost profit," the company said in a trading statement.
Its third-quarter earnings will be published in full on Oct. 30.
The euro was higher against the U.S. dollar and the British pound on Tuesday morning.
By 2:25 a.m. ET, the single currency was up 0.2% versus the greenback, after falling the previous day.

articles.title_orig: Apple ‘Welcome home’ event: Three new products are coming tomorrow
articles.title_zh: Apple ‘Welcome home’ event: Three new products are coming tomorrow
articles.content_orig:
Apple officially confirmed that it will hold a product launch event tomorrow, October 13. With a “Welcome home” tagline, the launch is expected to focus on new smart home products. Here’s everything to expect at tomorrow’s Apple event.
There are two components to the event, as Ryan outlined . There is the in-person experience for members of the press in New York City, as well as what Mark Gurman has called an “online video presentation.”
This suggests we can expect press releases and a video (or videos) to drop around 9 a.m. ET/6 a.m. PT on October 13. Apple hasn’t confirmed this, so the actual launch might vary. At a minimum, though, we know it will announce something on October 13, and some people will see it in person while the rest of us follow along from home.
Tomorrow’s headlining announcement will be Apple’s long-rumored smart display product, which Bloomberg says will be called HomeView . Apple believes that this product can serve as a central hub for your house, powered by Siri AI and Apple Intelligence.
According to Bloomberg , the device will have a 6-inch square display atop a half-dome base, with a metal arm holding it up. The HomeView will reportedly come in two variations: one that can be mounted on a wall and one that can sit on a countertop. Reports have likened the design to Apple’s iconic iMac G4 .
One of the flagship features of the HomeView will be its ability to recognize multiple people in a household. Mark Gurman reports that it can recognize who is talking to it or approaching it and dynamically adjust what’s shown on the screen.
In terms of software , the HomeView reportedly mixes different elements of the Apple Watch, Apple TV, and iPad. This includes iPad-like app designs and Apple Watch-style icons. It will also heavily borrow from the iPhone for widgets and StandBy mode .
Finally, while HomeView will be announced tomorrow, the latest reporting is that it won’t be available until sometime in November.
Apple is also expected to announce a new Apple TV 4K, its first update to the set-top box since November 2022. The new Apple TV will look the same as its predecessor, but it will reportedly include the A19 or A19 Pro chip.
That upgraded chip will allow Apple to bring Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features to the Apple TV for the first time.
The new Apple TV could also have built-in microphones for Siri interactions. The Siri Remote, meanwhile, might add a speaker to make it easier to find if you misplace it.
Apple is also reportedly working on new software features for the Apple TV and HomePod. For example, there are code references to a new feature that would let you arrange four full-sized HomePods in a surround sound system when paired with Apple TV.
The HomePod mini will also get its first proper upgrade tomorrow. The big change here will be a new S10 chip that is much faster than the current model’s S5 processor, bringing support for Siri AI. For context, the S5 chip used in the current HomePod mini is the same chip Apple debuted with the Apple Watch Series 5.
Beyond the faster chip, the new HomePod mini 2 will reportedly come in new colors:
Finally, Apple is working with LG on new “second-party” accessories for HomeKit. Apple reportedly collaborated with LG to co-develop products including a smart lock, thermostat, doorbell, and multiple cameras.
Bloomberg says Apple won’t release these accessories for “at least a few more months.” They could still be shown off as part of Apple’s broader home strategy tomorrow, though.
While we obviously have a pretty good idea of what Apple will announce tomorrow thanks to these rumors, I’m still really excited to see the company unveil its home roadmap. It’s felt like a category Apple has neglected for far too long, and one it might finally start taking seriously tomorrow.
What are you most excited to see at Apple’s “Welcome home” event tomorrow? Are you planning to buy the all-new HomeView or upgrade your Apple TV and HomePod mini? Let us know down in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Saudi warning system stayed silent before deadly airport attacks
articles.title_zh: Saudi warning system stayed silent before deadly airport attacks
articles.content_orig:
Houthi missile attack on Riyadh airport: Saudi Arabia vows resilience
The Saudi Arabia-led coalition fighting in Yemen has said its forces intercepted another ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as the city reels from attacks that have killed at least 14 people in recent days.
In a statement on X, Turki Al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the coalition, said the Houthis fired one ballistic missile at Riyadh and two towards Khamis Mushait, a city in the southwest.
All three were “intercepted and destroyed”, he said.
Residents of Riyadh reported several powerful explosions on Monday night, moments after a text message to their phones warned of an aerial threat.
The Houthis, who control Yemen’s most populous areas, including the capital, Sanaa, said their target in Riyadh had been King Khalid International airport.
Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said the group had also sent a drone towards a military airbase at Khamis Mushait, near the Yemeni border. He again warned international airlines and travellers “against operating flights to airports” in Saudi Arabia, except in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, saying the facilities were “unsafe”.
The renewed attacks came as King Khalid International airport in Riyadh remains closed after a Houthi attack on Saturday that killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 others. Another strike on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11.
Saudi authorities said the airport would remain closed until this Saturday, and airlines have canceled flights. The Houthis have also struck Saudi oil facilities.
The attacks come as the Houthis fight forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government for control of the country. The Saudi-led coalition has carried out an air campaign against the Houthis and backed the government’s ground forces. The fighting erupted amid regional tensions set off by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
Speaking at an energy conference in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud said the attacks on airports over the last week have tested the kingdom’s resilience.
“The events of recent weeks are serious,” the minister said. “Our response must be equally serious.” He added that Vision 2030, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plan to diversify the Saudi economy, “must continue. Investment must continue”.
Saudi authorities have meanwhile opened an investigation into why the country’s air defences failed to stop the barrage, according to two regional officials who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity. An initial inquiry found that the Houthis first launched several drones to clear a path for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles, which then reached the airport, the officials said.
The Houthis possess ballistic missiles with warheads that can change direction in flight, posing a challenge to the Patriot interceptors and other systems the Saudis rely on.
One official told AP that investigators also wanted to know why the defences had not given earlier warning of an attack in which missiles and drones flew more than 1,000km, or 620 miles, to reach Riyadh.
US President Donald Trump separately criticised the Houthis but gave no indication that Washington would intervene. “Well, the Houthis are misbehaving very badly. No good,” he told reporters when asked what he planned to do about the group.
A Houthi official warned that US involvement would bring retaliation.
“If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond; rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, told the AFP news agency.
Al-Bukhaiti also warned “all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets”.
The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom’s flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme.
The United Arab Emirates’s national carrier Etihad Airways announced on Monday that it was cancelling all flights to and from Riyadh until next week. It also suspended flights to Dammam and Jeddah.
Bahrain’s national carrier Gulf Air said it, too, was cancelling all Riyadh flights until Saturday.
US operator Delta announced it would delay the launch of direct flights from Atlanta to Riyadh, scheduled for October 23.

articles.title_orig: Data center boom puts Republicans in a bind before midterm elections
articles.title_zh: Data center boom puts Republicans in a bind before midterm elections
articles.content_orig:
A year ago, there weren't many voters talking about data centers. Now, the massive facilities being built to satisfy the enormous computing needs of the AI boom have become one of the most explosive issues of the 2026 midterms , and their construction is opening a divide between the Trump administration and Republicans running in state and federal races this fall.
When ChatGPT launched in late 2022, most data centers were being built in blue states. But by 2025, 68% of data centers online were in red states. Now, 75% of data centers under construction and 80% of data centers in the planning stage are in predominantly Republican states, according to new data from Cleanview Research, an independent energy market intelligence company tracking data center development.
"Red states have more of a history of accepting large, energy intensive, infrastructure projects — even those that might have detrimental effects on communities," said Chris Millay, a data center analyst at the macroeconomic consultancy Greenmantle. He also points to the relative lack of environmental regulation and the availability of open land as reasons rural states are receiving more investment.
President Trump sees the AI race as critical to the economy and national security, and he's one of data centers' biggest boosters. At a recent Ohio rally, he said of data centers, "We want them … look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio — you can't just turn them off. They'll go to China."
He has repeatedly dismissed public opposition to data centers, posting on Truth Social that "the only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor." Mr. Trump has also resisted regulation, though he has called on developers to give back to local communities through education, lower taxes, job creation and energy cost protections.
Red states may be hosting most of the boom, and increasingly, communities living next to data centers are pushing back. People who live near data centers have reported concerns about their property values, noise , higher energy bills and resource depletion. Meanwhile, calls for moratoriums are spreading through communities across the country.
Overall, opposition to data centers outweighs support by 30 points, with polls showing the majority of Republicans oppose the construction of data centers near them.
"It's such a consensus issue it's really impossible to take the other side," said Millay. "When voters see a politician who supports data centers, they think, 'Well, how am I going to trust him with my job?'"
Some of the president's closest allies have begun to break with him on the issue. In Texas, which has the most data centers under construction, GOP Gov. Greg Abbott has paused environmental permits and grid connections for new data centers. Abbott, who is seeking a fourth term, is in a surprisingly close race against Democrat Gina Hinojosa.
In Texas' tight Senate race , the Republican nominee, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, wants to end Texas' sales tax break for data centers. He has also said they should be held criminally liable if they power AI chatbots that endanger children.
Data centers seem to be the single issue where Democratic and Republican candidates sound nearly identical.
In Ohio, Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor, said in a press release, "I am calling on our Statehouse to pass a conditional moratorium on data centers."
Her GOP opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, has gone further. He vowed to "issue an executive order on my first day in office to immediately halt the approval of any new data center project announcements in Ohio," and to keep that pause in place until lawmakers pass his "Ohioans-First" law, which would require data centers to provide free electricity to surrounding residents.
A recent New York Times/Siena poll found that data centers are a weak point for Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted, with voters favoring his opponent by an 11-point margin on the issue.
Campaigns have spent $45 million this year on ads that mention data centers — most of them in opposition — according to AdImpact.
In Georgia, where candidates have spent nearly $13 million on ads mentioning data centers — more than any other state — the Republican gubernatorial candidate, Rick Jackson, is sticking with Mr. Trump. While the Democratic candidate, Keisha Lance Bottoms, is calling for a temporary moratorium on construction, Jackson says the decision should be left up to local officials.
Jackson made the case for data centers at a recent press conference, saying he wanted "to educate people on the benefit if they want [a data center]." Some counties, he said, expect they "will have zero property taxes after the data center goes in." Effingham County, where OpenAI plans a $20 billion data center, has pledged to use some of that revenue to cut homeowners' property taxes.
Because most of the next wave of data centers is largely planned in states Mr. Trump won in 2024, the choices Republican candidates make, siding with voters or with the president, could decide whether those projects are paused, made more expensive or even canceled.

articles.title_orig: US archbishop says Catholics in army should not participate in firing squad
articles.title_zh: US archbishop says Catholics in army should not participate in firing squad
articles.content_orig:
United States Archbishop Timothy Broglio has urged Catholics who are members of the country’s armed forces not to take part in a planned public execution by firing squad, saying that it violates the teachings of the church.
Broglio released a strongly worded statement on Monday raising a series of concerns about the US military’s plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army major who killed 13 people during a shooting attack at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.
“I oblige any Catholics assigned to the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church,” Broglio said.
He also asked whether the US wants to “imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries”.
The plan to livestream the execution on December 3 was announced last week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who characterised the spectacle as deterrence.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there are serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth told the right-wing media outlet Real America’s Voice.
But the proposal has sparked backlash from lawmakers , rights groups and critics who warn that a publicly broadcast killing is not only unethical but could also be used as anti-US propaganda.
Hasan, now aged 56, was shot by the police during the 2009 Fort Hood attack and is now wheelchair-bound. Critics fear livestreaming Hasan’s death could turn him into a symbol for armed groups that may be hostile to the US.
Cardinal Blase J Cupich, the archbishop of Chicago, also condemned the plan to livestream the execution in a social media post on Monday, questioning the example it could set for children.
“Capital punishment is unacceptable in any case,” he said. “The planned broadcast of the taking of a life by firing squad is nothing short of performative barbarism. Do we really want our children, who will inevitably view it, exposed to the pornography of a state-sponsored slaying?”
Hegseth has said he wants the execution to take place at the same time and location as the 2009 shooting spree, and described using military members to carry out the death penalty.
“It hadn’t been since World War II since we’ve done that,” Hegseth said of the firing squad. “Well, I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win.”
The last US military execution by firing squad was of Eddie Slovik, who was accused of desertion in 1945. He was the only US soldier to have such a sentence carried out for abandoning his post.
In Monday’s statement, Broglio also questioned the reasoning behind putting service members on camera to carry out Hasan’s death. He hinted that it could harm the US military’s image abroad.
“The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world,” Broglio wrote. “Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheel chair to the whole world?”
Without mentioning Hasan’s case specifically, Pope Leo also released a statement on Saturday condemning the death penalty.
“The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” he said in a social media post.
“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.”
President Donald Trump , who oversaw an unprecedented spike in federal executions during his first term in office, has approved Hasan’s execution.
Still, on Saturday, he indicated that he has not decided whether to proceed with a livestream.
“There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” Trump told reporters. “I’ll make a decision.”
Since the start of his second term as president, Trump has pushed for the increased use of the federal death penalty. In April, he also approved additional methods to carry out the death penalty, including the firing squad.
In the past, Trump has also floated the death penalty as a punishment for crimes ranging from drug dealing to sedition, a term he has invoked against political rivals .

articles.title_orig: Gravity and quantum information linked through a derivation of Einstein's equations
articles.title_zh: Gravity and quantum information linked through a derivation of Einstein's equations
articles.content_orig:
The paper, “From Quantum Relative Entropy to the Semiclassical Einstein Equations,” was authored by Philipp Dorau and Dr Albert Much. The “semiclassical Einstein equations” in the title describe a middle ground between two pictures of the universe: they keep spacetime itself smooth and classical, the way we experience it, while treating the matter that curves it according to the strange rules of quantum mechanics. This mixed description is currently our best tool for studying gravity in situations, such as near black holes, where a full theory of quantum gravity does not yet exist.
The new work builds on a celebrated 1995 argument by physicist Ted Jacobson, who showed that Einstein's equations can be derived by treating spacetime as a kind of thermodynamic system, with horizons behaving like heat-emitting surfaces obeying the ordinary laws of thermodynamics, much like a hot object radiating heat. Jacobson's derivation relied on classical concepts such as heat and entropy. Dorau and Much's work goes a step further: it derives Einstein's equations directly from quantum theory itself, with no classical assumptions built in from the start.
The key ingredient is quantum relative entropy, a measure borrowed from quantum information theory, the same field of study behind quantum computing, of how different two quantum states are from one another. The authors compared two situations: empty space with no matter in it, and the same space with matter added. The difference in information between the two turns out to match the energy of that matter. Since matter bends spacetime, this difference acts like a ripple in spacetime, and, combined with the known link between a black hole's surface area and its entropy, the shape of that ripple follows Einstein's equations exactly. It is a little like plucking a guitar string: matter is the pluck, spacetime is the string, and the note it sounds is Einstein's equations. The equations emerge on their own, without being assumed from the outset.
The result suggests that gravity, rather than being a fundamental force in its own right, may be a large-scale expression of quantum information: the more distinguishable two quantum states are near a horizon, the more spacetime itself must bend to accommodate them. It offers physicists a rigorous new path into ideas that have long circulated in the search for a complete theory of quantum gravity, connecting Einstein's century-old geometric picture of gravity to the modern language of quantum information.
Following its publication, the work drew attention well beyond the research community. It was featured on physicist Sabine Hossenfelder's popular YouTube channel, one of the most widely followed physics channels online, introducing the result to a broad international audience of science enthusiasts far beyond the pages of academic journals.
Dr Much, who has since joined the University of Sharjah, where he is involved in building a new research direction in quantum information, sees the result as part of a broader effort to understand gravity through the lens of quantum theory, a direction he intends to pursue further together with students and collaborators in Sharjah.

articles.title_orig: California beaches, homes slammed by waves from Tropical Storm Rachel
articles.title_zh: California beaches, homes slammed by waves from Tropical Storm Rachel
articles.content_orig:
By LAUREN ACTON-TAYLOR, US NEWS REPORTER
Published: 21:37 EDT, 11 October 2026 | Updated: 12:07 EDT, 12 October 2026
A powerful storm in California has battered waterfront property as monster waves whipped up by Tropical Storm Rachel tore away nearly 30 feet of a boardwalk.
A century-old boardwalk in Long Beach was seen being ripped apart by blistering winds and towering waves as pricey homes risk collapsing into the waters.
On Saturday evening, officials taped off the boardwalk with 'No Trespassing' signs as eight homes were red-tagged as unsafe to enter on the city's Peninsula, Mayor Rex Richardson said.
A ninth home was left yellow-tagged, allowing the home occupants access to grab their belongings but not stay in the property.
The tags, however, are not necessarily permanent. A red tag can be downgraded to yellow once repairs are made and inspectors approve the property, with inspections set to continue twice daily.
Officials are continuing to assess the threat and determine whether evacuation orders will be necessary as another round of severe weather looms.
Chilling footage on Friday night showed towering swells crashing against a home in the 6500 block of Seaside Walk, reaching its second-story windows as sections of the building and broken pieces of boardwalk drifted into the ocean.
Other images showed floodwaters engulfing nearby side streets and patios, pouring into homes and properties left badly damaged.

More recent video saw a structure being pulled off the ground, with two people attempting to claw it onto the ground until one of them was lifted from the floor, the California Post reported.
'It is not normal that we see this type of activity,' Mayor Richardson said on Saturday.
'Just in this season, this marks the third hurricane in just six weeks. We saw Hurricane Marie over Labor Day, which was followed soon by Hurricane Polo, and now Rachel is bringing with it more high tides, more surf, erosion that continues to cause damage to properties and damage along our coastline.'
'This is easily the most damage I have seen over the past couple of weeks,' said KTLA's Rich Prickett, whose crew captured the destruction from a helicopter overhead.
'Now the entire boardwalk is just starting to shred away, and now some of these homes are being impacted even more severely,' he added.
'As you’re seeing this house right here that’s starting to crumble as that erosion just continues underneath the house.'
The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning on Friday afternoon for Los Angeles County beaches until 3pm on Sunday, as forecasters expected waves reaching four to seven feet.
'It’s really heartbreaking to see how much has been affected with the surf and the high tides and everything. I mean, people are losing their houses,' Stacey Sniezak, Long Beach neighbor, told ABC 7 .
High tides over seven feet are expected in the mornings, as forecasters expect conditions may deteriorate on Sunday from strong winds, rain and elevated ocean water levels
Rain is expected to spread on Saturday night into Sunday morning, with showers possibly continuing through Tuesday night
Local officials distributed 7,600 sandbags in hopes of helping residents protect their properties

Sniezak said the damage to her home, where she has lived for 45 years, has left her devastated.
'It’s just impossible to fix at this point, and I don’t know how they’re going to do that,' she added.
Richardson announced all vehicle access to the Peninsula had been closed off for residents only, and added: 'We're encouraging everyone else to avoid the Peninsula all weekend, so that our city crews can have access and best perform this critical work.'
The Weather Service warned that coastal flooding could lead to damaged beach roads and structures, as well as significant beach erosion.
High tides over seven feet are expected in the mornings, as forecasters expect conditions may deteriorate on Sunday from strong winds, rain and elevated ocean water levels.
The Weather Service urged residents and visitors to stay off beaches, coastal walkways and vulnerable roads and structures. Motorists were warned not to drive around barricades or through floodwaters.
Rain is expected to spread on Saturday night into Sunday morning, with showers possibly continuing through Tuesday night.
Local officials distributed 7,600 sandbags in hopes of helping residents protect their properties.
'We’re looking at an unprecedented high tide, potentially 7.8 to 8 feet, which is significant for this area,' Long Beach Fire Department Assistant Chief Jake Heflin said.
'We’re not just talking about the peninsula, we’re not talking just about Naples, we’re talking about the potential for a citywide impact.'

articles.title_orig: World’s tiniest flowering plant could feed deep space astronauts
articles.title_zh: World’s tiniest flowering plant could feed deep space astronauts
articles.content_orig:
Duckweed on end of pencil. (University of Nottingham via SWNS)
The world’s smallest flowering plant would be an “ideal” food crop for future space missions , according to new research.
Duckweeds measure just a few millimeters across, but scientists say they could feed astronauts exploring deep space — as well as providing a potential source of food and protein on Earth.
Researchers at the University of Nottingham conducted gene expression analysis and cutting-edge microscopy on duckweeds.
Their findings, published in the journal Current Biology , show that they retain the same basic building blocks found in the shoots of larger plants.
But those structures have been “dramatically compressed” and fused together.
(Photo by Samiran Biswas via Pexels)
Study leader Anthony Bishopp says miniaturization is a “remarkable phenomenon” found throughout the natural world, from tiny animals to miniature plants.
He said: “Duckweeds are extraordinary flowering plants that can measure just a few millimeters across, yet their relatives include some of the largest herbaceous plants.
“We were interested to find out how a complete plant body plan can be packed into such a tiny space.
“While miniaturization in animals is often associated with the loss of organs or body structures, we have revealed that duckweeds have taken a different route.
“What surprised us is that, when we looked closely, the basic organization of the shoot was still there.
“Rather than throwing away parts of the blueprint, duckweed appears to have compressed and fused its components into an incredibly compact plant.
(Photo by Petr Ganaj via Pexels)
“That gives us a new way of thinking about how plants can evolve to become so small.”
Bishopp said duckweed research is advancing rapidly, driven by growing interest in the tiny plants as a potential source of food and novel protein on Earth, as well as a possible crop for future space missions.
He added: “Unlike most of the crops we grow today, which have been shaped by thousands of years of domestication and selective breeding, the potential of duckweed remains largely unexplored.
“Even the basic architecture of the duckweed plant has remained something of a mystery.
“Understanding how its body is organized provides an essential framework for understanding how duckweed grows, develops and functions — and ultimately how its potential might be improved.”
Study co-author Alex Ware said: “Duckweeds are astonishingly small, so it is tempting to think of them as either primitive plants or simply as having lost parts, but this is not the case.”
Ware added: “Our research adds to growing evidence from across the research community about this plant and will help efforts to turn them into a future crop.”

articles.title_orig: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: How a gold-buying spree helps the yuan go global
articles.title_zh: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: How a gold-buying spree helps the yuan go global
articles.content_orig:
Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Beijing. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses.
Buying gold every month for nearly two years is just part of China's plan to narrow a gap with the U.S. on holdings of the precious metal. What does that do to the yuan?
China's decades-long push for yuan internationalization is getting a lift from the buildout of Hong Kong as a gold trading center — denominated in the Chinese currency.
"As those trading volumes grow, there would be a growing volume of the physical gold trade that is denominated in RMB and not linked in USD," said Charles Chang, managing director and Greater China country lead for corporate ratings at S&P Global Ratings.
The Chinese yuan, also known as the renminbi, accounts for a fraction of international transactions in a global financial system dominated by the U.S. dollar. Analysts I spoke with don't expect major changes to that dynamic anytime soon, but Beijing's gold purchases and Hong Kong trading platform are just the latest steps toward supporting greater use of the yuan globally.
"The challenge with internationalizing the RMB it's somewhat more challenging to find places where you can use the RMB," Chang said. "In terms of gold particularly, if the RMB that the buyer receives can be converted to gold, then it gives more channels for the spending to be done."
Hong Kong, home to one of the world's largest stock exchanges, last month confirmed its efforts to develop a yuan-denominated gold market .
In a major move last year, the special administrative region of China linked its gold vault with one in Shanghai , allowing physical gold delivery to international institutions in Hong Kong denominated in yuan.
Over the next three years, Hong Kong plans to expand the capacity of its Shanghai-linked gold vault from 150 tonnes to over 2,000 tonnes , S&P's Chang pointed out.
That's nearly as large as all the gold reserves in China , he added. "If Hong Kong is able to complete this transaction, then it would become of the largest gold trading centers in the world."
The U.S. still has the largest gold reserves in the world at over 8,100 tonnes, according to World Gold Council figures for the second quarter. China held about one-third of that at over 2,300 tonnes.
"China's 23-month gold buying streak reinforces the credibility of the renminbi's internationalization drive," said Hao Zhou, head of research and chief economist at Guotai Junan International in Hong Kong.
"By steadily increasing gold reserves, Beijing is strengthening the long-term backing of its financial system and reducing reliance on dollar-denominated reserve assets," he said. "While gold alone will not determine the RMB's global role, it enhances confidence in the currency and supports broader efforts to expand its use in trade, investment and official reserves."
Gold accumulation by China and other countries' central banks will help reduce global reliance on U.S. Treasurys and U.S. dollar reserves, said Xia Yingying, head of the precious metals and new energy research group, at Hangzhou-based Nanhua Futures. That's according to a CNBC translation of the Chinese.
"This will suppress the U.S. dollar's premium from being a core reserve currency, and raise the risk premium associated with the dollar regarding credit, fiscal policy and sanctions," Xia said. "In the medium to-long-term it will gradually weaken the U.S. dollar's monopolistic position in the global reserve system."
China's growing gold purchases, however, also come as U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday named gold-standard supporter Judy Shelton as a senior advisor focused on China .
The Asian economy's rise as a manufacturing powerhouse benefited from the U.S. decision to abandon the gold standard more than 50 years ago. "With the delinking of the dollar and gold, and the consequent rise in the oil price, western manufacturing became less economic, and capital went to Asia in search of cheap labor and overall lower costs," wrote the central bank research group OMFIF in 2021.
While China is the largest consumer and producer of gold, it is just one of many developing economies that has expanded its reserves since 2022, according to S&P. The World Gold Council showed Poland has increased its gold reserves by more tonnes than China.
The trend goes beyond financial transactions. Like with rare earths, Beijing's gold ambitions start with control of some of the product.
China has acquired major gold mines across Latin America, Africa and Asia, according to S&P Global Ratings.
"China's plans for gold and its activities in gold are comprehensive and long lasting. These trends are going to be in place for a number of years," Chang said.
"The comprehensive nature of this," he said, "is something that markets often miss."
DeepSeek considers doubling latest funding round to up to $15 billion, sources say
China's DeepSeek is considering expanding its latest funding round to as much as 100 billion yuan ($14.9 billion), double its earlier target, with state-backed funds and corporate investors jostling for stakes, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. AI startup Manus raises $500 million from IDG Capital and others, indicating investors aren't deterred by Beijing's unprecedented order to block Meta's short-lived $2 billion acquisition.
China and Europe agree to halve Chinese hybrid vehicle exports
European trade commissioner Maroš Sefčovič said Friday that China has agreed to halve its exports of hybrid cars to the bloc. China's auto market is on track for its worst year since 2021, with sales down by more than 20% over roughly the first three quarters of the year, according to China Passenger Car Association data as of Sept. 27.
After a yearslong slump, China's real estate market may be set for a turnaround
Residential real estate prices may hit a bottom in the third quarter of 2028 , S&P Global Ratings said. It added that prices in China's largest cities, such as Beijing and Shanghai, will likely recover as soon as next year.

articles.title_orig: AM Broadcasters in Chile Face a Dilemma
articles.title_zh: AM Broadcasters in Chile Face a Dilemma
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › Columns and Views › Guest Commentaries
The author is a broadcaster and director of Radio Romance in Santiago, Chile.
AM radio is facing a crisis that can no longer be explained simply by declining audiences. The deeper problem is technological, economic and regulatory.
Without clear pathways to evolve, many stations risk disappearing. I am writing here about stations in Chile, but the discussion will have resonance anywhere AM radio is used.
For decades, AM radio was one of Chile’s most important communications platforms. It informed communities during earthquakes, accompanied listeners through the night, carried sports, news, music and conversation, and reached places other media could not.
Today, however, AM broadcasters are competing in a radically different ecosystem with technology that has lost much of its commercial appeal and, in many places, its listening convenience.
What should an AM station do in order to survive? The answer seems obvious: migrate.
Migration does not necessarily mean abandoning radio or erasing its history. It means allowing broadcasters to test new technologies, explore other bands, integrate effectively with digital platforms and find sustainable models that can preserve their role.
The alternative is much harsher: disappearance.
Chile should address this as a communications policy issue, not merely as a series of isolated problems affecting individual stations. When a broadcaster faces economic distress, loses access to a transmission facility or is forced to suspend operations temporarily, public policy should at least ask what tools exist to help a legitimate broadcaster adapt.
Today, Radio Romance is off the air on its terrestrial signal. We maintain only a minimal digital presence, with a basic music stream, so that Radio Romance does not disappear completely.
But this stream does not replace the radio station we built, nor does our current website reflect the full reality of what Radio Romance was and what we want to rebuild.
For a broadcaster, silence on the dial is extraordinarily painful.
Radio Romance has a history, an identity, an audience, thousands of hours of content and, above all, the determination to continue. What we do not have today is a technological bridge that would allow us to move from an AM model that has become increasingly difficult to sustain toward a viable future for broadcasting.
Other communications technologies have gone through managed transitions. Television moved from analog to digital. Telecommunications networks evolved. Mobile technology changed repeatedly. The answer to technological obsolescence has rarely been simply to let operators disappear.
Radio deserves the same discussion.
Chile has seen experimental broadcasting experiences involving AM operators and the lower FM band. If such experiments exist, it is reasonable to ask what criteria govern access, how another broadcaster may apply and what mechanism allows a traditional AM station to present a serious technology-transition project.
This is not about giving frequencies away.
It is not about eliminating technical requirements or ignoring the state’s legitimate role in managing scarce spectrum.
It is about something more basic: making the rules known and giving broadcasters an opportunity to be assessed under them.
We have asked the regulator for an opportunity to present and evaluate experimental alternatives that could offer a different technological path.
Our experience is bigger than the future of one station.
It reflects the situation of an industry that needs answers.
An AM broadcaster should not have to choose only between remaining indefinitely on an increasingly difficult-to-finance platform or disappearing.
There should be a third option: evolve.
Broadcasting also has a characteristic that is easy to overlook when viewed only through financial metrics: when a media outlet disappears, a voice disappears with it. A company may close, but when that company is a media outlet, an editorial, cultural and social window closes too.
That is why the future of AM is also a question of media pluralism. We do not need to preserve technologies artificially out of nostalgia. Nostalgia is not public policy. But technological change should not eliminate media outlets that still have experience, audiences, content and a willingness to continue simply because no bridge was built to the next technological environment.
That bridge deserves serious discussion.
Further, the disappearance of AM radio has a human dimension that can hardly be measured in numbers.
For decades, every station was surrounded by an entire ecosystem of technicians, operators, engineers, broadcasters, journalists, producers and collaborators who made it possible for a human voice to travel hundreds of miles.
Many devoted 30 or 40 years of their lives to this profession. Today, when an AM station ceases operations, they do not simply lose a job. They discover that the knowledge and experience accumulated over a lifetime have fewer and fewer places where they can still be put to use. Behind every transmitter that goes silent are professionals, collaborators, and families confronting the gradual disappearance of the working world to which they once belonged.
On the other side of the receiver, something equally painful is happening.
Thousands of adults and older listeners grew up with these stations. For decades, they listened in their homes, cars, workshops and across the countryside. For them, radio was never merely a means of communication. It was companionship, routine, familiarity, and memory.
Saying that these audiences can simply move to the internet does not solve the problem. Many older adults are unfamiliar with apps and digital platforms; others, even when they know how to use them, cannot find the voices and programs that became part of their lives.
There is also a profoundly symbolic image: enormous antennas and transmitting facilities standing motionless in fields. Places once alive with technicians at work, transmitters operating day and night, and signals traveling across vast territories are now falling silent, often with little realistic possibility of ever being used again.
It is the gradual end of an entire ecosystem: people, professions, trades, listeners, memories, antennas and transmitters.
When an AM radio station goes off the air, the silence is not confined to the dial. It also remains with those who devoted their lives to making that radio possible — and with those who spent a lifetime in its company.
The solution may involve experimental technologies, new spectrum arrangements, digital broadcasting, hybrid radio and online distribution, and regulatory mechanisms that allow existing broadcasters to submit credible transition projects.
The important first step is to acknowledge the problem.
For much of AM radio, time is no longer measured in decades.
It may be measured in years — and for some operators, perhaps months. The question Chile should be asking is simple: Do we want to manage the disappearance of AM radio, or manage its transformation?
Those of us who have spent our lives in broadcasting are not asking for privileges.
We are not asking anyone to give us a frequency. We are asking for the opportunity to transform. Because when technology changes, there are ultimately two paths: migrate or die.

US chip production relies on ‘vulnerable inputs hidden deep in upstream global supply chains’, SIA says
China accounts for about 5 per cent of the equipment and materials directly supplied to the US chip industry when measured by country of manufacture, but its grip on certain rare earths needed for chipmaking is over 90 per cent, according to the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA).
While 95 per cent of the nearly US$27 billion annual spending by American chipmakers on manufacturing equipment and materials was sourced from companies headquartered in the US, Europe, and Japan, that figure dropped to 68 per cent when the value is counted by country of origin, according to SIA.
Suppliers “often rely on production chains outside their country of domicile”, the SIA said in a report published on Friday.

articles.title_orig: iPhone Duo: Apple To Debut Special Extra For In-Store Buyers
articles.title_zh: iPhone Duo: Apple To Debut Special Extra For In-Store Buyers
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
If you’re eager to get your hands on the highly anticipated iPhone Duo , the first foldable iPhone, here’s how to get a head start on ordering. Apple has opened a staging page for preorders on apple.com , where you can get ready to place a preorder for the viral phone.
Head over to Apple’s online storefront, and you’ll find that a new iPhone Duo configurator is now live. On that page, save your preferred phone color, storage, mobile carrier and payment method. Saving these details in advance ensures you can complete your purchase immediately when preorders open at 5 a.m. PT on Friday.
Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo , one of its first new products under the helm of new CEO John Ternus, during its Surprise and Shine event in Cupertino, California, on Friday. It’s the first foldable from Apple, although merely the latest in a wave of new bendy phones to hit the market.

Pricing starts at $1,999 for the 512GB model and tops out at $3,199 for the 2TB version — before carrier subsidies — making the iPhone Duo the most expensive iPhone ever released. Price aside, observers expect demand among early adopters to be high, so prepping your order now is a smart idea.

articles.title_orig: Government spent $10 million on pro-Trump ads after president said super PAC would fund
articles.title_zh: Government spent $10 million on pro-Trump ads after president said super PAC would fund
articles.content_orig:
President Trump leaves the stage after speaking during an election rally in Syracuse, New York on Oct. 9, 2026. Alex Wong/Getty Images hide caption
Ads promoting President Trump and his policies continued to be paid for by the U.S. government well after Trump announced he would have his MAGA Inc. super PAC take over funding the ads and kept airing despite a federal judge ordering them to come down.
An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer dollars has been spent to air the ads since the campaign began in late September. Nearly $10 million of that total was spent after Oct. 5, when the president pledged to fund it privately in a post on Truth Social .
"The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump posted at the time. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc."
The ads have been criticized by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle with Republicans praising the president's choice to shift funding for the ads to an outside super PAC. But, that praise was premature. Despite giving the impression that there'd been a policy change, the government-funded ads didn't stop airing after Trump's post.
The White House has repeatedly referred to the ads as public service announcements, but a lawsuit filed by Common Cause and others argued they were being funded without congressional approval and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda produced with taxpayer dollars.
The ads — five of them in all — cover a wide range of pro-Trump content. One includes a splashy montage of photos of the president with a chorus singing "love me" serving as the soundtrack. Another is an exact duplicate of an ad made by the Trump campaign during the 2024 election cycle. Two promote the military operations in Venezuela and Iran. All of them end with the words "Paid for by the U.S. Government" on the screen.
The spots continued being broadcast for several hours after a federal judge overseeing the lawsuit issued a temporary ruling Sunday night saying the government "shall cancel or cause to be cancelled any slot, placement, reservation, or arrangement for the airing or dissemination of the challenged advertisements, including those placements for the evening of October 11, 2026."
Pro-Trump spots aired hundreds of additional times Sunday night into the wee hours of Monday morning.
"The last PSAs paid for by the government aired yesterday evening," a White House official not authorized to speak publicly told NPR on Monday afternoon, adding that the government "did not receive notice from the court in time to cancel the ad buys. The PSAs will be paid for by outside groups moving forward."
The White House had previously said that taxpayer funds used for ads would not be reimbursed. The White House has also insisted these ads were merely about promoting patriotism. They argued the ads can't be campaign related because the president isn't running for office this year and have nothing to do with the midterm elections next month. But Trump has repeatedly implored voters to vote like he is on the ballot and his dismal approval ratings have been dragging down Republicans all over the country.
A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found the ads are pretty unpopular. The poll asked whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to use "taxpayer funds to pay for election-related television ads featuring the President or members of his cabinet." It wasn't even close, with 86% of Americans saying it is inappropriate. Even 80% of Republicans said the ads were inappropriate.
It's rare to get such bipartisan agreement on anything these days.

articles.title_orig: World-famous science educator Bill Nye believes in Titans: ‘You're going to change the world’
articles.title_zh: World-famous science educator Bill Nye believes in Titans: ‘You're going to change the world’
articles.content_orig:
When the first notes of the “Bill Nye the Science Guy” theme song began echoing through the Titan Student Union Portola Pavilion, students didn’t miss a beat. They sang along to the popular chorus — “Bill, Bill, Bill, Bill, Bill, Bill” — as the world-famous scientist and educator took the stage for the “Beyond the Conversation” series at Cal State Fullerton.
Hosted by Associated Students Inc., the signature series invites notable speakers to campus to share their stories and spark dialogue among students. Bill Nye, who spoke to the Titan community on Oct. 7, joins a star-studded lineup of previous “Beyond the Conversation” speakers, including Olympic swimmer Michael Phelps , Oscar winner Ke Huy Quan , and Emmy and Grammy Award-winning actress Cynthia Erivo .
As the co-creator and host of the Emmy Award-winning ’90s television series “Bill Nye the Science Guy,” Nye has emerged not only as an entertaining educator but also as an influential advocate for science and facts in an era of misinformation.
His lifelong commitment to advocacy has earned him various honors, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, inclusion in the Time 100 Health list, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, and a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Children’s & Family Emmy Awards.
Nye has made science and engineering education entertaining and accessible for generations of viewers. He shared his story with Cal State Fullerton students and imparted a few pieces of advice and encouragement to help them on their academic journey.
Getting a college education gives you a way of looking at the world that is essentially priceless. You are going to go out there and dare I say it, change the world.  — Bill Nye
“You guys are going to graduate from Cal State Fullerton with this degree, and it will be worth more the day after you graduate than the day you graduate. I guarantee you,” Nye said.
“Getting a college education gives you a way of looking at the world that is essentially priceless. You are going to go out there and dare I say it, change the world.”
With the rapid expansion of social media and artificial intelligence, Nye acknowledged that students have access to a wealth of information about science, the environment and sustainability. He said the key to consuming and identifying reliable information is critical thinking.
As a scientist who has spent his career asking questions and investigating the wonders of the world, Nye said critical thinking isn’t about questioning everything and assuming everything is wrong. It’s about evaluating evidence before deciding if a claim is true.
“What we want everybody to embrace is what is nowadays called critical thinking. It used to be called logic or logical reasoning, but we want everybody to be in the habit of evaluating evidence,” Nye explained.
For students who are preparing to launch their careers, Nye said it’s important to lead with passion and curiosity and to take that first step.
“My advice is to just get started. You don’t know where it’s going to lead, but find something you want to do or something that you wouldn’t mind doing, and get started,” Nye said.
“The thing that goes wrong is when you have so many things to do, you just can’t get going. Just get started. You’re going to change the world.”
Nye was interviewed by Nathan Hoang, a fourth-year business administration student and student programmer for ASI’s student programs and engagement team.
“Events like ‘Beyond the Conversation’ inspire students to see themselves in these figures and empower them to believe maybe they can one day be on that stage as well,” Hoang said. “What stood out to me about Bill’s interview was how he kept the conversation fun, but still didn’t shy away from pointing out our responsibilities as young adults and the potential we have to shape the future.”

articles.title_orig: 39-year-old unvaccinated woman becomes 6th measles death in Pennsylvania
articles.title_zh: 39-year-old unvaccinated woman becomes 6th measles death in Pennsylvania
articles.content_orig:
A 39-year-old unvaccinated woman in Franklin County, Pennsylvania, has become the sixth person to die of the highly infectious virus amid a state outbreak that has stricken over a thousand people since it began in April.
The woman died on Saturday, October 10. She had several underlying health conditions and had recently tested positive for measles, according to an advisory posted on social media by Franklin County Coroner Jordan Conner. The advisory noted that the woman’s death meets the definition of a measles death set by the state’s health department.
In an emailed statement to The Washington Post , the coroner’s office said the primary cause of death was listed as “probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles.”
The previous five deaths amid the state’s measles outbreak included a newborn , a 6-week-old , an 18-year-old , a 20-year-old , and a 40-year-old . All the deceased were unvaccinated; the two infants were too young to have been vaccinated.
As of the latest measles update from Pennsylvania’s health department on Friday, October 9, there have been 1,136 cases in the state since the start of the year—1,124 of which are from the current outbreak. Overall, 218 people have been hospitalized. The outbreak, which now spans 41 of the state’s 67 counties, shows no signs of slowing. There had been 157 new cases reported just in the previous week.
A spokesperson for the state health department told the Post that it is “aware” of the new death and is reviewing the case. It will provide an update once the review is complete.
Measles, declared eliminated in the US in 2000, is roaring back amid misinformation and slipping vaccination rates. The nationwide measles case count for the year has hit 4,080 , the highest total since 1991. Pennsylvania’s outbreak is also the largest on record since that year . The US is widely expected to lose its measles elimination status when experts from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) meet in November to review US measles data.
Under anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has only included two of the six deaths so far in its reporting. There were three measles deaths reported in the US in 2025. Prior to those deaths, there had not been a measles death reported in the country since 2015.

articles.title_orig: Emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed by confusion after failed execution, 911 calls reveal
articles.title_zh: Emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed by confusion after failed execution, 911 calls reveal
articles.content_orig:
Emergency call records have revealed the confusion that developed among prison staff and emergency call handlers after the execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike went wrong last month in Tennessee.
Pike, 50, who killed Colleen Slemmer alongside her then-boyfriend in 1995, was given two doses of lethal injection on 30 September. Once it became clear that she was not going to die from the dosage, she was taken to hospital.
The confusion resulted in part from an apparent disconnect between prison staff, according to the AP news agency, which first obtained audio of the emergency calls.
This allegedly delayed Pike's treatment. The BBC has asked the state corrections department for comment.
The department has not yet stated what it thinks went wrong in the attempted execution of Pike. Pike's legal team has offered the explanation that the pentobarbital chemical, with which she was injected, probably spread under skin rather than reaching her bloodstream in a sufficient quantity to kill her.
Pike has now been discharged from hospital, though in their most recent update on her health, her team cautioned that she faced a "long road to recovery". It is not clear what treatment, if any, she is receiving now that she is back in prison.
Her case is now in uncharted territory as she is thought to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
Slemmer's mother, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death, has branded the failed execution a "mess".
Pike's boyfriend at the time of the murder, Tadaryl Shipp, remains in prison, having been spared the death penalty because he was not yet an adult when the crime was committed.
The sequence of events on the evening of 30 September was pieced together by US media using a combination of emergency call recordings and transcripts. The records were published in full by the Nashville Banner news outlet.
The initial call made from Riverbend Prison - which was reportedly made at 20:40 local time - was considered to have been false by first responders, after the caller was unable to verify themselves using a code.
That person seems to have been in a part of the prison where the injections were taking place. They said: "We've been carrying out an execution tonight. We've administered 10 grams of pentobarbital. The person is not yet deceased. That started approximately one hour ago. And we're calling for an ambulance."
The Nashville Department of Emergency Communications released records of its conversations with other local agencies as it tried to confirm whether the call was genuine.
The confusion appears to have been compounded by other prison staff, from the institution's central command, who said at 21:07 that they "would have been the ones to call in" and that they "did not make that call".
It was not until about 21:11 that prison officials verified that the initial call, made about half an hour previously, had in fact been genuine. At that point, the emergency responders were allowed through the prison gates.
A later call acknowledged that the situation had been chaotic. At 21:34, as Pike was being taken to hospital, one medic asked a colleague to ensure the prison knew where Pike was being taken, "just 'cause there's been so much other confusion".
Pike's lawyers are yet to comment on the recordings.
Over the course of last week, her team provided frequent updates on Pike's condition - detailing how she had regained her ability to walk and talk before ultimately being discharged from hospital care.
It is unclear whether or when the state will try again to execute Pike. Some state Republicans have called for a new method to be attempted. Pike's legal team, meanwhile, are calling on Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute her punishment to the lesser sentence of life in prison without parole.
For now,  Lee has paused the state's executions for the remainder of the year. An investigation is taking place into what went wrong with Pike's execution.
The head of the state's corrections department is resigning from his post in the wake of the botched execution.

articles.title_zh: 61-year-old woman holds plank for 5 hours in quest for new world record
articles.content_orig:
DonnaJean Wilde held a plank for five hours at the Huntsman World Senior Games earlier this month in Utah. It could be a new world record for longest plank held by a woman. But why does she do it?
And now, a world record attempt that's pretty hard to believe. DonnaJean Wilde, 61 years old, held a plank for exactly five hours at the Huntsman World Senior Games earlier this month in Utah.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED CROWD: Four, three, two, one.
CHANG: Now, for those of you who are unfamiliar, a plank is an abdominal exercise where you hold your body in a rigid, straight line all the way from your head to your heels, supported only by your forearms and toes. Wilde already held the record for longest plank held by a woman, at four hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds. And she says she almost didn't make it past that mark this time.
DONNAJEAN WILDE: When I got to four hours and 30 minutes, I really did hit a wall. But with 10 minutes left or 15 minutes left, the CEO of the games, Kyle Case - he was on the mic, and he had that whole crowd cheering me, and that's why I made it through.
CHANG: Wilde's five-hour plank is currently under review by the experts at Guinness World Records. She says her love of the plank began about 15 years ago, when she had just broken her arm.
WILDE: I couldn't plank for very long - like, a minute, a minute and a half - but it was something I could do with a cast on, a broken wrist.
CHANG: But when the cast came off, she kept planking, and she kept getting better at it.
WILDE: And then my family - my kids, my husband - they said, you know, Mom, people don't do this. They don't get on the floor and just plank. So maybe you should, like, think about going for a record or something.
CHANG: Now, I know what you guys are all thinking out there. Why would someone choose to plank for so long? Well, for starters, Wilde says this kind of prolonged exercise gives her the same kind of rush as a runner's high. But also, she says, it's a good opportunity for multitasking.
WILDE: I completed a whole master's degree while I was planking, wrote all my papers. And I actually wrote a book.
CHANG: She is not kidding. She has apparently mastered the skill of typing on her laptop while propped up on her elbows, planking.
WILDE: As a teacher, so much of my life has been just trying to encourage people to find something that they love and then repeat it, because that just changes your brain.
CHANG: DonnaJean Wilde is pretty good at pushups, too, by the way. She once did 1,575 pushups in an hour, which was also a world record for a while. She says she might try and break that record again if she can find herself to take a break from all that planking.
(SOUNDBITE OF HVNSENT SONG, "SAVED MY SOUL")
