articles.title_orig: Nikon revokes first prize in Small World in Motion video competition over AI use
articles.title_zh: Nikon revokes first prize in Small World in Motion video competition over AI use
articles.content_orig:
The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified after organizers concluded that his use of generative AI broke the rules.
Ning Xu was named the winner of the annual Nikon Small World in Motion competition in September, but his video received a number of critical comments from experts who questioned its use of AI.
Nikon launched an investigation, and announced its conclusion in a statement Friday.
“After thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel, Nikon has determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI,” the statement reads, adding that the competition rankings have been adjusted.
“This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition. It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent,” it said.
Nikon also said it would revisit its rules and evaluation procedures for the annual competition in future.
The new winner is a video showing a tiny roundworm and a single-celled Dileptus, a kind of single-celled microorganism, by Vietnamese researcher Nguyen Nam Nhat.
Xu’s video captures the abnormal beating of airway cilia — hairlike structures that protrude from cells within the human body — in a child living with primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), a rare genetic disorder.
When Nikon posted the video on LinkedIn, it attracted criticism from scientists such as Edward Phelps, an associate professor at the University of Florida, who said there were “many serious problems with this video.”
Winner of Nikon microscopy photo contest faces criticism over AI usage
Phelps said that some of the biological structures shown in the footage do not behave as expected. “The microscopy community deserves an explanation from Nikon,” Phelps added.
In response, in a series of comments on LinkedIn, Xu acknowledged that he had used AI.
“AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion,” he wrote.
“It was applied afterwards to the reconstructed grayscale data to distinguish and color structures with similar morphology,” he added.
CNN has reached out to Xu, who now works at the National University of Singapore as a research fellow, for further comment.

articles.title_orig: Sea World starts building marine wildlife hospital on Gold Coast
articles.title_zh: Sea World starts building marine wildlife hospital on Gold Coast
articles.content_orig:
New facility will care for sick and injured marine wildlife
Construction is underway on a new world-class marine wildlife hospital at Sea World in Australia
Construction is underway on a new world-class marine wildlife hospital at Sea World on Australia's Gold Coast.
The new Sea World Foundation Wildlife Hospital is expected to open next year and will serve as the Southern Hemisphere's first facility of its kind.
It will provide specialist care for sick and injured marine wildlife , including dolphins, whales, dugongs, rays, turtles, seabirds and sharks.
Purpose-built for rapid rescue and rehabilitation, the new facility will feature specialist equipment to treat larger marine mammals.
Queensland’s environment minister Andrew Powell said: “Shovels are in the ground at Sea World, with work underway on a world-class marine wildlife hospital that will give more sick and injured wildlife the specialist care they need."
As well as caring for marine wildlife, the hospital will give Sea World visitors the opportunity to see marine conservation and rehabilitation for themselves.
"This is a win for wildlife and a win for Queensland, supporting wildlife rehabilitation while creating new education opportunities and showcasing our conservation efforts to millions of visitors each year," Powell added.
Sea World is owned by Australia-based theme park operator Village Roadshow Group.
The new Sea World Foundation Wildlife Hospital is expected to open next year on the Gold Coast Sea World Foundation
Village Roadshow Group 's CEO Clark Kirby said: "For more than 30 years, Sea World has been at the forefront of marine rescue and rehabilitation efforts around Australia, and this project will allow our team to have an even greater impact on Australian marine life.
“The state-of-the-art facility will allow our specialised veterinary and marine animal experts to help more animals and educate the millions of guests who visit Sea World on conservation efforts to minimise impacts on the environment."
He added: “We have already rescued hundreds of marine animals this year, ranging from whales, dolphins, dugongs, turtles, seabirds and sea snakes, and with marine wildlife being under more threat than before, this new facility will greatly expand our capabilities.”

articles.title_orig: Love blooms on a hostile colony world in As You Wake, Break the Shell
articles.title_zh: Love blooms on a hostile colony world in As You Wake, Break the Shell
articles.content_orig:
Love blooms on a hostile colony world in As You Wake, Break the Shell
Sci-fi author Becky Chambers on designing believable ecosystems, balancing scientific accuracy with emotional impact and emphasizing empathy over spectacle
By Sam Macdonald edited by Sarah Lewin Frasier
One of science fiction’s oldest themes is its insistence that the future isn’t inevitable. Few contemporary authors embody that idea more than Becky Chambers , whose stories imagine alternative futures—not through grand revolutions or galaxy-spanning battles but through ordinary people trying to care for one another.
As a defining voice of the “hopepunk” genre, Chambers has built a reputation for science fiction that prizes empathy as much as imagination. Her latest novel, As You Wake, Break the Shell , brings us to the hostile, unpredictable world of Fortune, where acid rain falls and billowing volcanoes shroud the horizon. The story follows a reclusive botanist and a spacefaring pilot across alternating timelines as they search for connection and purpose, attempting to navigate a life where Fortune has never favored the bold.
We caught up with Chambers to discuss a toxic planet’s world-building, scientific accuracy in storytelling and the motivational merits of unrelenting spite.
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
[ An edited transcript of the interview follows .]
This story spends a lot of time on a colony planet with a poisonous atmosphere. What does designing an ecosystem teach you about designing a civilization?
Everything. It’s really important for me to start with what the environmental conditions are because that’s going to affect everything from what we’re eating, what we’re building houses out of, what kind of clothes we have—and all of those things, in turn, affect culture. There is so much about our values, our personalities, that are actually molded by the physical environments we exist in, both natural and constructed.
Starting from [the questions] “what do we have” and “what do we not have” is really important for me. Suppose someone’s eating a sandwich. What’s in the sandwich? It’s a throwaway line that seems like it doesn’t matter, but it’s actually really important to say whether or not there’s lettuce in this sandwich, because that does communicate a lot of information about how this world works.
For this book, I had a really big table of crops [to reference], what are we growing, how are we growing it, what’s available and what’s not?
Those are details I spend a lot of time sussing out before I really get into the thick of drafting the story.
What specific ideas inspired the scientific foundation for this story?
Botany is the big one. I have always had an appreciation for plants but not any actual sort of technical knowledge about what it is that I’m looking at. So I did a lot of research for this book into how plants work, and specifically into seeds, which is a topic I have become fascinated by the more I learn about it. Seeds are a big part of this book, as are plants and the way they communicate with each other.
How does scientific accuracy influence your storytelling? Do you often find yourself molding the plot to fit the science, or vice versa?
I look at science as partially a foundation but more of a tool that I use to color the world that I’m in. I want it to feel tangible and possible, but I’m very willing to take some liberties here and there for the sake of getting the feeling across.
I tend to think of what I’m doing as more like impressionism than photorealism. If you think of something like Monet’s Water Lilies, for example, it doesn’t look like a real pond, right? But it feels like a real pond. And I often use a similar approach with my work. I am not necessarily painting you a picture of the cosmos as it actually exists, but what I’m trying to communicate is the sense of wonder and awe that I feel when I’m experiencing those things in the real world. So it’s a matter of getting the emotional quality of discovery across, and sometimes that does mean taking shortcuts.
With As You Wake Break the Shell , I kept it within the realm of “with sufficient technology, this could be possible.” Is it probable? Probably not. There are a lot of things that I gloss over because they’re not things that everyday people outside of science would know about or understand. We know [in the reality of the story] that there are giant space-dwelling creatures out there. We don’t need to know how it is that they evolved or what kind of world it is that they came from. Those are questions that interest me as a person who is into real science, but they don’t serve the story.
This book has a knack for taking the unknown and making it feel familiar while making the familiar feel unknown, simply by showing it from a new perspective—for instance, that of an enormous, cargo-toting space behemoth. How do you get into the headspace of examining humanity from the outside?
It’s a highly technical process that involves me sitting in my armchair and just staring at the ceiling and thinking about what it would be like to have a body other than mine, and just sort of deconstructing everything that makes me down to the raw components and trying to figure out what it is that’s necessary and what’s not.
I take a lot of inspiration from the natural world. I have a really keen interest in invertebrate life and in deep-sea life, and I have a real interest in animal intelligence that exists in nonmammalian creatures.
What would it mean to communicate through color? What would it mean to communicate through pheromones? What does the world feel like if you don’t have a sense of sight like we do? I just love taking any one of those traits and then expanding it to make something that we would recognize as a person, regardless of whether they physically look like us or not. How does that make you think about yourself? How does that make you think about existence?
As You Wake, Break the Shell is a love story as much as a space story. What did pairing those genres let you explore that you couldn’t do with either one on their own?
It allowed me the freedom to not segment any of the things I was thinking of into separate boxes. This was a really personal book for me in that I’m writing about everything I care about in this one. I’m writing about the natural world, I’m writing about society, and I am also writing about love, romantic love, and these are all things that are extremely important to me in my everyday life.
We have a bazillion stories about “and then they lived happily ever after,” but I actually want to see what that looks like because it’s never that simple.I feel that the most interesting parts of a relationship are what happens “after,” and so that was what drove a large part of my decision to have [the book] be a split timeline, where it’s very clear from the jump that they’re going to be together a long time and we’re going to see all these different stages in what makes them them, because I do think that that’s an area that is underexplored.
You’ve said before that you write the stories that you need to hear. What did you need to hear from this book?
I wanted to see a relationship that matched my own. Queer representation in media is better than ever in a lot of ways, and yet it’s still very rare to see anybody over their 20s.
By the time we started getting more stories about coming of age or people falling in love when they’re young, I was already too old for those stories. I was feeling a real frustration in not finding love stories that spoke to me where I am now in my life. It was one of those things of, “I guess I’ll just have to write it myself.”
Your work has been described as “wholesome,” “thoughtful” and “heartwarming.” How much of your inspiration and motivation actual

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Quantum-Computing Company IonQ to Buy Cybersecurity Firm for Up to $1.3 Billion
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Quantum-Computing Company IonQ to Buy Cybersecurity Firm for Up to $1.3 Billion
articles.content_orig:
College Park, Md. - Oct. 12, 2026 - IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), the world’s leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Elisity, Inc., a Zero Trust security company, in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion. The acquisition brings together IonQ's post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) capabilities with Elisity's enterprise Zero Trust technology platform. On a combined basis, IonQ will benefit from an expanded cybersecurity platform that both uncovers and protects against present LLM and emerging quantum threats.
Elisity builds on IonQ’s expanding quantum security offerings with a high-growth enterprise security business, cutting-edge Zero Trust technology platform, and team of industry leaders led by cybersecurity expert CEO James Winebrenner. Elisity has a strong track record of doubling its revenue and its customer base year-over-year with zero churn among deployed customers. With more than 100 global customer deployments and deep CISO and security community relationships, Elisity will provide IonQ with expanded channels to bring its PQC, QKD and quantum computing offerings to market for both enterprise and government networks, opening up the more than $10 billion microsegmentation opportunity with double-digit CAGR to IonQ.
“With Elisity and its team as part of IonQ, we will be well positioned to help customers protect critical infrastructure and enterprise networks throughout the transition to the quantum era. As I said first, Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted. IonQ is offering its customers a vertically integrated full-stack quantum platform across quantum computing, networking, sensing and cybersecurity. Just as adding SkyWater Technology expanded IonQ’s capabilities in chip design, fabrication and packaging, Elisity will bring proven enterprise policy enforcement scale and deployment experience to our quantum security strategy and will give IonQ a strong growth platform to serve customers and create value for our shareholders,” said Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ.
“Our customers need to prioritize post-quantum cryptography initiatives while securing existing assets to keep essential operations running,” said James Winebrenner, CEO of Elisity. “With IonQ, we will be optimally positioned to partner with them to modernize their crypto-agility programs, accelerate post-quantum cryptography capabilities while advancing their holistic Zero Trust posture and deploy hybrid-cybersecurity solutions today that are prepared for the quantum future.”
Elisity’s Commercial Advantage
Enterprises face two overlapping priorities: containing attacks that operate at machine speed and preparing to protect sensitive information against future quantum threats. The urgency of this transition is underscored by recent White House executive orders advancing quantum innovation and accelerating the federal government's migration to PQC. These directives reinforce the importance of securing critical systems and preparing government networks for quantum-era threats while supporting long-term modernization.
Today, Elisity IdentityGraph combines native asset identity and partner-enriched context, and risk information to inform least-privilege access policy for users, devices, workloads and AI agents. Teams can simulate policies before limiting each identity to the communications it needs, helping reduce attack surface and contain an attack’s spread. By bringing together Elisity's Zero Trust framework with IonQ's PQC and QKD capabilities, the companies will combine cryptographic protection for sensitive information and communications with identity-based controls that limit unauthorized access and the spread of threats across enterprise networks. The shared roadmap with IonQ will extend IdentityGraph with cryptographic inventory and risk information. This integrated approach will help customers address quantum-related security risks through a multiyear transition while strengthening defenses against current cyberattacks, including threats involving AI agents.
Following closing, Elisity will continue serving its customers under its current leadership, including current CEO James Winebrenner. Together, the companies will continue their track record of innovation, customer success and strong partner relationships, backed by IonQ’s demonstrated approach of investing in the critical technologies it acquires.
IonQ’s Multiproduct Revenue Growth Opportunity
IonQ brings an established track record in growing its quantum security and quantum-secure communications offering. The company has deployed some of the largest quantum-safe national communications networks in the world, including in Switzerland, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, and serves global customers with quantum-safe defense in depth spanning quantum-safe posture management, quantum key distribution, and post quantum cryptography.
Customers are increasingly adopting multiple IonQ products and services, driving growth in multiproduct revenue and providing evidence of demand for integrated solutions; in the second quarter of 2026, IonQ delivered 40% year-over-year growth in multiproduct revenue..
IonQ and Elisity expect opportunities to cross-sell complementary security solutions, expand relationships with enterprise and government customers, and develop integrated offerings.
Under the terms of the agreement, IonQ will acquire Elisity in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion, including up to $150 million in earnout opportunity subject to performance of the Elisity business. The number of IonQ shares to be issued in the transaction will be calculated at closing based on the volume weighted average price of IonQ common stock for the 20 trading days prior to, but not including, the third business day before the closing date, but that price will not be greater than $49.61 or less than $33.07 per share.
The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of required regulatory approval.
Elisity helps enterprises advance Zero Trust security for users, devices, workloads, AI agents and other non-human identities. Elisity IdentityGraph correlates identity, asset and risk information from native and partner sources to inform access decisions. Elisity’s software policy layer uses the network to enforce access rules independently of the underlying network technology. Teams can simulate policies and limit each identity to the communications it needs, extending the value of existing network and security investments. Founded in 2019, Elisity has a global employee footprint and a growing number of customers in the Fortune 500. Learn more at elisity.com .
IonQ, Inc . [NYSE: IONQ] is the world’s leading quantum platform and foundry - delivering integrated quantum solutions across computing, networking, sensing, and security. IonQ’s newest generation of quantum computers, the Superion, is the latest in a line of cutting-edge systems. Earlier systems have helped customers and partners including Amazon Web Services, AstraZeneca, and NVIDIA achieve a 20x performance increase over previous quantum solutions and accelerate innovation in drug discovery, materials science, financial modeling, logistics, cybersecurity, and defense. In 2025, the company achieved 99.99% two-qubit gate fidelity, setting a world record in quantum computing performance .
Headquartered in College Park, Maryland, IonQ has operations across North America, Latin America, EMEA, and APAC. Our quantum computing services have been available through all major cloud providers since 2021, while we also meet the needs of networking and sensing customers across land, sea, air, and space. IonQ is making quantum platforms more accessible and impactful than ever before. Learn more at IonQ.com .

articles.title_orig: Rise in poverty is ‘a wake-up call for the world’, UN development chief says
articles.title_zh: Rise in poverty is ‘a wake-up call for the world’, UN development chief says
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
The number of people living in “multidimensional” poverty has risen for the first time in 15 years, reaching 1.2 billion, as families struggle to meet their basic needs.
The finding comes in the 2026 update of the global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) published by the United Nations Development Programme ( UNDP ) and Oxford University, which measures overlapping hardship across health, education and standard of living.
The 1.2 billion figure represents 51.5 million more people than in the 2025 update .  Of this number, more than half are children – 617 million – and 83 per cent live in rural areas.
“The rise in poverty should be a wake-up call for the world,” said UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo.
“Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable.”
The index was developed in 2010 to measure poverty beyond what people earn.
It examines 10 indicators of health, education and standard of living, such as nutrition and child mortality, years of schooling, and access to electricity, drinking water and sanitation.
A person is considered “multidimensionally poor” if they are deprived in one-third or more of the indicators.
Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia account for the overwhelming majority of deprivations across every indicator.
The 2026 update – which covers 108 countries, representing some 78 per cent of the global population – reveals that the increase in poverty is partly due to population growth outpacing efforts to improve living standards.
In 95 countries where no new survey data was available, updated population estimates increased the number of people counted as poor by nearly 16 million.
The remainder of the increase comes from 13 countries where data was gathered, reflecting the genuine change in poverty incidence and the associated demographic change, as well as differences in indicator coverage.
The updated surveys also revealed a mixed picture on the ground. Five of these countries – Egypt, Nepal, Tajikistan, Angola and Zambia – have reduced the share of people living in multidimensional poverty, however population growth outpaced poverty reduction in both Angola and Zambia, meaning that the total number of people living in poverty still increased.
Meanwhile, Nigeria provides an example of how fragile progress in tackling poverty can be. Although the country made significant reductions in multidimensional poverty in the 2010s, both the poverty rate and the number of people struggling to make ends meet have increased.
The international community has pledged to reduce the proportion of people living in poverty by at least half before the end of this decade, in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
The authors of the 2026 MPI update believe that this target is achievable.
“We know progress is possible,” Mr. De Croo insisted. “Countries that have tackled these challenges together, rather than in isolation, have shown what determined action can achieve.”
UNDP reported that 33 countries have halved their MPI value in fewer than 15 years, including six in sub-Saharan Africa. In Eswatini, the share of people living in multidimensional poverty has fallen from nearly 39 per cent to eight per cent.
Meanwhile, China recorded the fastest reduction among countries with available data by halving its MPI value from 9.5 per cent to 4.2 per cent in just four years (2010-2014).
The shows that many countries continue to make progress, with some reducing poverty rapidly and at scale, underscoring both the urgency of renewed action and the possibility of success, the agency said.

articles.title_zh: IT'S BACK. THAT'S BIG. The All-Electric smart #2 Makes Its World Premiere at the Paris Motor Show
articles.content_orig:
HANGZHOU, China , Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- smart today celebrated the World Premiere of the all-new smart #2 at the Paris Motor Show, marking the return of its iconic two-seater for a new electric era.
Thirty years ago, the smart vehicle was presented as an art object beneath the Louvre Pyramid. Today, smart returns to Paris with the fully realised production smart #2.
Mr. Tong Xiangbei, Global CEO of smart, said: "The smart #2 is more than the return of a familiar silhouette; it is a demonstration of what our teams can achieve in the most demanding urban segment. Its World Premiere in Paris, followed by launches in Europe and China, opens an important new chapter for our global product family."
Mr. Kang Yi, Global CMO of smart, said: "The smart #2 expresses our core D.N.A. in a very pure way: Designed with Love, No Compromise on Safety, and Amazing Drives. It is small in footprint, but big in personality."
An Icon for a New Generation
Styled by the Mercedes-Benz Global Design Team, the smart #2 translates the character of smart's iconic two-seater into a contemporary new form, guided by its design philosophy of Love, Pure, Unexpected.
Clean proportions, short overhangs and its signature wheels-at-the-corners stance preserve the pure smart silhouette and maximise space. Unexpected details, including logo-inspired lighting and a contemporary interpretation of the iconic floating roof, reinterpret familiar smart cues.
Inside, bench-style seating and S-shaped cockpit make efficient use of the compact cabin, while carefully considered colours, materials and distinctive details bring warmth and individuality.
The Split Tailgate features an upper glass that opens independently in tight spaces, and a lower section that folds down as a loading platform or a 120-kg capacity seat.
smart #2 Couture Edition: Function becomes Fashion
As a surprise highlight, smart also unveiled the exclusive smart #2 Couture Edition, carrying the established "Function becomes Fashion" theme from concept to production.
Limited to 999 units in Europe and 999 units in China, the Couture Edition combines an Atelier White Matte exterior finish with a contrasting Platinum Gold roof, distinctive gold detailing and exclusive 16-inch Lyra rims. A numbered interior badge further underlines its limited-edition character.
Purpose-Built for Urban Mobility
Underpinning the smart #2 is the newly developed Electric Compact Architecture (ECA) platform, engineered specifically for smart's ultra-compact all-electric two-seater.
Measuring 2,746 mm in length, the smart #2 maximises usable space within its ultra-compact footprint. The ECA platform brings together intelligent packaging, a floor-mounted high-voltage battery, rear-wheel drive and advanced chassis technology.
Power comes from a rear-mounted 60 kW electric motor delivering 130 Nm of torque to the rear wheels.
For Europe, the smart #2 features a 35.8 kWh LFP battery, with a target combined WLTP range of 290 km. Supporting 65 kW DC fast charging, the smart #2 can charge from 10% to 80% state of charge within 20 minutes, while AC charging at up to 11 kW supports convenient everyday charging.
A curb-to-curb turning circle of just 6.95 metres makes navigating tight city streets and narrow parking spaces effortless.
The smart #2 features a five-link rear suspension, a first in its class, supporting confident and composed driving both in cities and on highways.
Central to the smart #2, the Tridion Cell Evo creates a robust protective structure around the passenger cabin without compromising the vehicle's compact dimensions. The vehicle also comes equipped with driver-assistance technologies including smart Pilot Assist and Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) with Stop & Go and Highway Assist.
The smart #2 Begins Its Global Market Rollout
Following its World Premiere in Paris, early ordering for the smart #2 will begin in Europe and China, bringing smart's iconic two-seater to two of the brand's key markets.
For Europe, the smart #2 will initially be offered in three core trim lines — Pure, Pure+ and Premium — alongside the limited Couture Edition.
For China, the smart #2 will be unveiled in Premium and Couture Edition variants.
Market-specific line-ups, pricing, specifications, equipment and availability will be communicated locally.

articles.title_orig: Sen. Marshall pays bakery bill after complaint goes viral
articles.title_zh: Sen. Marshall pays bakery bill after complaint goes viral
articles.content_orig:
Republican Sen. Roger Marshall settled his debts this weekend with a bakery in Kansas after a bill for hundreds of treats his campaign ordered for a 2020 event sat unpaid for six years.
Holly Thomas, the owner of the shop that made cookies, brownies and cupcakes for Marshall’s primary election watch party, said in a social media post on Friday that she will not vote for the senator in this year’s election, where he is facing an unexpectedly strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, after he failed to pay the $678.75 he owed her small business.
“This isn’t about political parties or policy disagreements. It’s about my personal experience as a small business owner and the importance of honoring financial commitments,” Thomas said. “That experience is why Roger Marshall will never get my vote.”
Thomas said she reached out several times but never heard back, noting that the lack of payment came as her business was just beginning and at the height of the coronavirus pandemic. “Six years later, I haven’t forgotten,” she said.
Marshall posted a screenshot of a payment for $1,300 on Saturday, showing that he had paid the half-a-decade-old cookie bill, and then some.
“We have absolutely no idea how this happened, but rest assured as soon as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020, double,” Marshall said on social media.
Thomas confirmed a few hours later that she can “finally mark the invoice paid.”
​The Republican senator is facing a competitive reelection race this fall, with voters’ strong disapproval of President Donald Trump and widespread economic anxiety raising the possibility that Kansas could send a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in nearly a century. A recent poll by The New York Times and Siena University showed Marshall tied with Hamilton at 45% among likely voters.
The repayment of the bakery bill come as Marshall, a former obstetrician-gynecologist, has faced criticism over a report last month that he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid medical debt.
The New York Times found that he had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills and at least 81 of those individuals were arrested for missing court dates. Democrats have leaned on the story in ads, accusing Marshall of disregarding people’s concerns about healthcare costs.
A spokesperson for Marshall told the Times that the longtime doctor spent many years treating patients regardless of their ability to pay.
“Judges issue warrants when people repeatedly miss court dates, not doctors,” spokesperson Payton Fuller said in a statement to the outlet.

articles.title_orig: Judge orders the Trump administration to cancel taxpayer-funded promotional TV ads
articles.title_zh: Judge orders the Trump administration to cancel taxpayer-funded promotional TV ads
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads as an illegal misuse of funds. She told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night, in granting a temporary restraining order.
“Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements” during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said.
Asked for comment, the White House referred to an Oct. 5 social media post from Trump in which he defended the taxpayer-funded ads as “rather standard” but, amid backlash, said he would pay for them from his political fundraising. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because “the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow.”
The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million in taxpayer money for the ads. Legal experts have suggested that violated a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda” and potentially other laws.
“We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda,” the plaintiffs said in a statement issued by Democracy Forward, the nonprofit legal organization that represents them. “There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.”
In a court declaration Saturday, senior DHS official Holly Mehringer wrote that the money came from funds appropriated by Congress that are “available for, among other things, ‘commemorating efforts and events related to border security.’”
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs.
The ads, which began airing in late September, glorify Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms. One features a clip of Trump talking about the threat of communism and another is a replay of an ad from his last presidential campaign. The fifth ad in the campaign began airing Tuesday, focusing on the Trump administration’s capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro .
The use of public funds to pay for the ads drew heavy criticism — including from some in the GOP.
“It shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters.
The Democratic National Committee has separately sued the Republican administration over the ads.
Amid the backlash, Trump said he would start paying for the ads with a campaign account. A White House official said there were no immediate plans to reimburse the government for money already spent.
Associated Press reporters Collin Binkley and Ali Swenson contributed.

articles.title_orig: Linus Torvalds "Did What I Preach", Used AI To Make Code Decipherable & Uncovered More Bugs
articles.title_zh: Linus Torvalds "Did What I Preach", Used AI To Make Code Decipherable & Uncovered More Bugs
articles.content_orig:
PRAGUE – Many open-source developers still dislike AI. The latest example is System76 banning AI-generated content from its COSMIC desktop . At Open Source Summit Europe , Linux creator Linus Torvalds offered a different take: “I actually really like using AI,” Torvald told Dirk Hohndel, his good friend and head of Ericsson Software Technology , in their latest discussion.
Also: 5 reasons why Linux will dominate desktop computing
But that enthusiasm comes with a distinction worth keeping in mind. Using AI to make a hobby project more enjoyable is one thing. Using it responsibly in the Linux kernel, where generated patches and bug reports can overwhelm maintainers, is  another.
Torvalds said, “I think that you need to be very careful using AI when you’re doing something real and important.”
Torvalds explained he hadn’t always felt that way about AI programming. “I used to think it was just not very good — but now I’m at  the point where I actually really like using AI.”
“To be fair,” he continued, “I don’t do a lot of kernel programming. I’m a maintainer. The Linux kernel is a project where other people do the real work, and I act as the collection point. But I still enjoy programming immensely. I think AI is a wonderful tool if you use it correctly and treat it as a tool, and I find it makes programming much more enjoyable.”
Torvalds recalled, “I started programming in 1981 or so, and back then computers were much simpler, and you could understand what they were doing, and also the programs you compared your own programs to were much simpler.”
Also: The 6 AI-free Linux distros I recommend most
“It’s a different story today,” Torvalds said. “The bar in software engineering has grown so high that it’s hard to see your own small efforts as worth anything, because you’re used to all these polished, professional programs. “
“A lot of people make fun of vibe coding, but I think it’s a wonderful way to find joy in programming. It makes you feel like you’re doing something relevant. It allows you, as a new programmer, to do things that you would otherwise have a really hard time with.”
He continued: “I love the concept of AI as a gateway drug because I was working on my own toy project, the guitar pedal , and I knew what I was doing. I had a user interface that I had written myself in C that was running on a microcontroller that was running on this small screen, and I was like, “This is just stupid. It looks like something from the ’80s; I wanted it to look like something from this century. But I don’t do Java. I do kernels.”
Also: My 5 favorite Linux distros for security
“So, I use AI to do the things that I’m bad at,” Torvalds went on, “I’d seen all the same YouTube videos you have. Give AI a prompt, and it will do it. So I gave it a prompt, and it did it, and it was horrendous. Then I said, ‘Hey, look! I already did this in C. I did it the right way. It’s just ugly.”
That’s not to say AI isn’t useful for finding and fixing mistakes in the Linux kernel. Hohndel asked about Sashiko , an agentic Linux kernel code review system. Torvalds said its public reviews now appear on the Linux Kernel Mailing List (LKML) . Indeed, some subsystem maintainers now expect patches to have received such a review before accepting them.
That doesn’t mean all pull requests have to go through an AI review. Some maintainers do require it, though, and it seems likely that all will eventually require it.
Also: I doubted this mini PC could handle my local AI tasks, but it blew me away
AI tools can identify genuine security problems. They can also surface issues in old, no-longer-used drivers that have gone unnoticed for years. Torvalds sees value in the resulting fixes, while acknowledging their cost. “It is, I think, improving our code base… Although it is also stressing maintainers out to the point that it’s a problem.”
As Torvalds said in Mumbai earlier this year. convincing but fabricated bug reports can require substantial human effort to disprove, while narrowly targeted patches may fix one symptom without addressing the underlying problem. Torvalds called some submissions “mindless band-aid kind of patches.”
That said, AI code checking is here, and it’s here to stay. For example, Torvalds said, “three-quarters of the preceding day’s Linux Kernel Maintainer Summit discussion concerned making AI generation and review less stressful and more useful. The bottleneck isn’t getting patches. It’s getting useful work through review without exhausting the people responsible for it.
Because it was Linux’s 35th anniversary , Torvalds also talked about how the process of making Linux has changed over the years. In the beginning, Linux had no development infrastructure at all to speak of. Instead, Torvalds tracked changes through tarball patches and regularly distributed updated source code.
“I made patches every single day internally, and I released them at least weekly,” he recalled. “And it actually worked surprisingly well for a small project.”
Also: ‘I’m not a programmer’ anymore: Linus Torvalds on the only two tools he uses now
Hohndel noted that the distribution of new tarballs and their accompanying changes continued until 2002, when Linux had become a much larger undertaking. Back in those days, Torvalds said, “It was really just me, myself, and my computer.”
His reluctance to adopt existing source-control tools was not simply stubbornness. He wanted developers to work independently, with their own local environments. “I really felt very strongly that everybody should have their own local setup,” he said.
As I explained in my 2025 account of Linux’s growth , drawing on Jonathan Corbet’s history of the project, Linux’s openness attracted an expanding development community. But relying on Torvalds to apply incoming patches manually became a bottleneck. Accepting contributions by hand was no longer enough; the project needed a better way to integrate them.
The BitKeepe r version control system provided that improvement, although its proprietary licensing divided the kernel community. Some developers refused to use it. Torvalds, however, found that distributed source control made it substantially easier to merge work from subsystems such as networking and ARM. Torvalds said, “BitKeeper, as far as I’m concerned, was a huge success.”
He didn’t consider it flawless. Rather, it showed him what source control could do and helped him identify what he actually wanted. Nor did its adoption require every maintainer to use the same tool.
Also: Linux after Linus? The kernel community’s plan for replacing Torvalds
Then the 2005 BitKeeper licensing dispute took away the tool he had come to depend on.   After experiencing distributed source control, returning to the old approach was no longer appealing. Git was Torvalds’ answer .
Hohndel recalled that Torvalds took 11 days to produce the first working version: a new object model, code, and a functioning tool in under two weeks. The early Git was not universally popular. Developers accustomed to CVS found it unfamiliar, and its first versions had rough edges.
Its eventual success still surprises Torvalds. Today, according to a 2022 Stack Overflow Developer survey , Git has become the de facto standard for version control: Nearly 94% of respondents, and almost 97% of professional developers, use Git. All Torvalds wanted was a tool for Linux, not to remake software development everywhere. As he put it,  “I sometimes get way too much credit for Git.”
After roughly six months, he handed over its maintenance. His point was that the subsequent decades of development belonged to other people, not that the initial work was unimportant. “It’s worth noting that Git today is a lot better than Git in 2005.”
Linux’s release process underwent another major change, moving away from long-lived, separate stable and development trees toward frequent releases, a merge window, and release candidates.

articles.title_orig: Republican US senator facing re-election settles six-year bakery debt
articles.title_zh: Republican US senator facing re-election settles six-year bakery debt
articles.content_orig:
Roger Marshall says he has ‘no idea how this happened’ and repaid bill double for 2020 election watch party treats
The Republican US senator Roger Marshall says he has finally paid off a bakery debt – after six years and repeated collection attempts reported by a Kansas business that had supplied a large order of treats for a 2020 election watch party.
“We have absolutely no idea how this happened”, the Kansas senator wrote in a social media post containing a screenshot of the payment on a $678.75 invoice from Holly’s Sweet Treats as well as his $1,300 payment. “And we have repaid the bill … double.”
Word of Marshall’s cookie debt became widely known after an 8 October social media post from Holly Thomas, a baker from Hutchinson, Kansas, which began: “Do you know why I will never vote for Roger Marshall?”
The Holly’s Sweet Treats proprietor recounted how Marshall’s campaign had “ordered cookies and treats from my bakery” for a 2020 primary election watch party that preceded his winning his first six-year Senate term.
“For nearly a year,” the post continued, “I made repeated attempts to collect payment, reaching out by phone and email. I never received a return phone call, and the invoice was never paid.”
Thomas said that unpaid invoice was particularly challenging because it was during the Covid-19 pandemic, “when small businesses everywhere were struggling just to keep their doors open”.
“Every single dollar mattered,” Thomas wrote. “Those cookies and treats cost money to make, employees’ time to prepare, and resources that my little business couldn’t afford to give away.”
Thomas concluded: “Six years later, I haven’t forgotten. This isn’t about political parties or policy disagreements. It’s about my personal experience as a small business owner and the importance of honoring financial commitments.
“That experience is why Roger Marshall will never get my vote.”
Thomas’s post achieved internet virality and unsurprisingly caught the attention of Marshall’s camp.
By Saturday, Marshall had published his own social media post addressing Thomas’s statement, saying on X: “As some folks may have seen, there was a post on social media regarding an unpaid 2020 cookie bill.
“We have absolutely no idea how this happened, but rest assured as soon as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020, double.”
Marshall’s post – along with the picture of the paid invoice to Holly’s Sweet Treats – quickly drew a community note from X users aiming to provide what the platform characterized as additional context.
“Multiple attempts to get paid were ignored,” the community note said, linking to Thomas’s Facebook post.
Many users gave Marshall what they considered his just desserts in the form of harsh comments, with one commenter saying: “You got caught, and that’s the only reason you paid.”
Others calculated that he actually owed Thomas more than $1,400 at 18% simple annual interest for six years. And one noted that $678.75 doubled is $1,357.50 – not $1,300.
Thomas on Saturday published another Facebook post that acknowledged Marshall’s having “paid his bill”.
“Better later than never, right?” Thomas wrote. “Six years later, I guess we can finally mark that invoice PAID!”
Marshall’s response to Thomas’ publicizing his late payment unfolded in a political climate which has the Democrats favored to win control of the US House during the 3 November midterms .
Polls more recently have shown that the Democrats also have a relatively viable chance to win US Senate seats in states that traditionally elect Republicans and possibly gain a majority in that chamber, too – given Donald Trump’s unpopularity amid high living costs and the war in Iran that the president helped start alongside Israel.
Marshall’s announcement about paying Thomas also arrived after the Cook Political Report amended its prediction for his November re-election run against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton from leaning in the Republican’s favor to being considered a toss-up.
The announcement from Marshall – a physician – about the tardily settled bill also came after the New York Times reported in September that his obstetrics-gynecology practice had sued hundreds of patients over the years in connection with unpaid medical bills, including for as little as $101.

articles.title_orig: Huawei in collaboration with China Unicom and Peking University Win 2026 Leading Lights Award, Advancing 5G Free-Mobility Private Network to a New Era in Higher Education
articles.title_zh: Huawei in collaboration with China Unicom and Peking University Win 2026 Leading Lights Award, Advancing 5G Free-Mobility Private Network to a New Era in Higher Education
articles.content_orig:
Light Reading, the globally recognized authority in communications industry media, has announced the winners of its 22nd Leading Lights Awards. The " Peking University CARSI 5G Free-Mobility Private Network " jointly submitted by Huawei, China Unicom, and Peking University, stood out among 151 shortlisted projects worldwide, winning the Outstanding Use Case: Network Security & Resilience Use Case Award. This recognition marks a new chapter in the application of 5G private networks within the higher education sector. As AI-driven research and digital campus life accelerate across universities, faculty and students are placing greater demands on campus networks. Previously, access to internal campus resources relied on the traditional internet + VPN model. This approach carries security risks, including data leakage and account compromises. It also delivers a poor user experience, with high latency, unstable connections, and repeated login prompts. These shortcomings no longer meet the needs of modern universities. At the same time, conventional 5G private networks suffer from lengthy service provisioning cycles and elevated management costs. They are ill-suited to the high personnel turnover typical of academic institutions. Breaking through the security and experience bottlenecks of traditional VPN models  and enabling faculty and students to access campus resources securely and conveniently from anywhere outside campus  has become a shared priority in university IT modernization. In response, Huawei and China Unicom have jointly introduced the " Peking University CARSI 5G Free-Mobility Private Network " solution  directly addressing the security risks and experience gaps faced by faculty and students accessing campus intranet resources from off-campus locations. The solution delivers a seamless upgrade in campus resource access: no VPN cluster, no annual licence planning, no SIM approval workflow. Zero-Touch Onboarding: Built on CARSI (Campus Authentication and Resource Sharing Infrastructure), the federated authentication system of CERNET (China Education and Research Network), faculty and students can activate the 5G Mobile Private Network using their existing university credentials. A single phone  without changing SIM cards or phone numbers  provides seamless access to the campus network, eliminating the need to install or repeatedly start and stop VPN clients.
Light Reading judges commented: This architecture  The university, not the operator, remains the sole identity authority  carries significant replication potential. The solution leverages the existing CERNET infrastructure without requiring large-scale campus network modernization, and can be rapidly deployed across the universities already connected to CARSI. The 5G Free-Mobility Private Network is now officially live at Peking University, covering the core scenario of off-campus access to campus intranet resources. Faculty and students enjoy seamless campus network access with a single phone  no SIM change, no number change. During a three-month pilot involving over 100 faculty and students, more than 70% of respondents rated the new service as superior to traditional VPNs in stability, latency, and ease of use. Service provisioning time was reduced from several days to seconds, and the private network deployment cycle was compressed from approximately three months to three weeks. This solution provides a replicable model for 5G private network deployment across the universities connected to CARSI, with the potential for international extension. Looking ahead, Huawei will continue to deepen joint innovation with China Unicom across more universities  focusing on 5G-Advanced, 6G, network security, and AI-native networks (AIDN)  to advance the network-as-a-service vision in the education sector. By helping quality educational resources transcend campus boundaries, Huawei is committed to contributing a China-based solution and Chinas wisdom to global university digital transformation. FAQs: Q1: What is CARSI? CARSI (Campus Authentication and Resource Sharing Infrastructure) is a unified identity authentication platform built by CERNET (China Education and Research Network). It now covers over 1,000 universities across China, enabling cross-institutional identity mutual recognition and resource sharing. Q2: What problem does the 5G Mobile Private Network solve? Traditionally, faculty and students must install VPN clients to access campus intranet resources  a process that introduces security risks and delivers a frustrating experience. With the 5G Free-Mobility Private Network, users reach the campus network seamlessly through China Unicoms 5G service. No new SIM card, no number change, no additional setup is needed. The system also resolves the management overhead caused by frequent faculty turnover and the continuous cycle of student enrollment and graduation, automatically terminating access when users leave the university. Q3: What application scenarios does the 5G Mobile Private Network currently support? The 5G Mobile Private Network is now officially live at Peking University, enabling faculty and students to access campus intranet resources using 5G data from off-campus locations. In the future, this solution can be rapidly replicated across the more than 1,000 universities connected to CARSI, and can extend to overseas universities through eduGAIN.

articles.title_orig: Around the World in Explorer Names
articles.title_zh: Around the World in Explorer Names
articles.content_orig:
At the Explorers Club, uptown, the American Geographical Society, founded in 1851, celebrated its hundred-and-seventy-fifth year one recent evening by observing its most sacred ritual: a ceremonial globe signing. The society’s Fliers & Explorers Globe, donated in 1929 by the Times editor and A.G.S. president John Finley, was signed by many of his era’s most renowned explorers, including Charles Lindbergh, Amelia Earhart, and Sir Edmund Hillary. “Finley interviewed people who came in from their expeditions, and he’d get them to sign it,” Jerome Dobson, an A.G.S. president emeritus, said. His necktie had an antique-map print. Later, the globe was signed by John Glenn, Neil Armstrong, the Apollo 8 crew, and others. That night, it would be signed by the oceanographer, former Navy captain, and retired astronaut Kathryn Sullivan—the first person to both walk in outer space and visit the deepest point of the ocean, in the Mariana Trench.
During cocktail hour, a spiffily dressed group of eminent geographers gathered in the library bar around a Fliers & Explorers replica—a party globe, perhaps. “This is the globe you can touch,” Marie Price, the current A.G.S. president, said. “Spin it around!” (“Let’s not go wild,” Dobson said.) The library had an icy-exploration theme: taxidermied polar bear, signed Shackleton portrait, Admiral Peary’s ice pick, snowy painting of bedraggled men by a tent. “That looks like one of our camp trips, huh, Lee?” Price said to Lee Schwartz, a former GOTUS (Geographer of the United States).
When Dobson joined A.G.S., in 1997, the Fliers & Explorers Globe was underappreciated, he said. “I didn’t even notice it,” he recalled. “It was on a spindly shaft in the corner; we’d go spin it.” It hadn’t seen much action since Glenn had signed it, at the White House, in front of J.F.K., Lyndon Johnson, “and two of Bobby Kennedy’s children—not the one currently in government.” Seeing an opportunity, Dobson had proposed new signings. “Who wouldn’t consider it an honor?” he said. “So we invited Neil Armstrong; Don Walsh and Jacques Piccard, the first people to go to the bottom of the Mariana Trench; and Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones, who first circumnavigated the globe in a balloon.” (Were the Piccards inspiration for Captain Picard, of “Star Trek”? “I never thought of that,” Price said.) The retired Coast Guard captain Lawson Brigham, who resembled a seafaring Lee Iacocca, approached the globe. “I signed through the Bering Strait, but I had been at the North Pole and the South Pole,” he said, pointing. “As close to the South Pole as you get on a Coast Guard icebreaker.”
“Lawson did the circumnavigation pole to pole, not the most common way to go,” Price said. “You need an icebreaker.” (“There is a precedent—names on here of pilots who went that way,” Dobson said.) Nearby, wearing a waterproof modern-adventurer hat, the eighty-five-year-old G.P.S. pioneer Charlie Trimble chatted about trying to determine whether Mt. Everest was rising or sinking. (Rising, he said.)
During the main event, in a ballroom, Sullivan, a capable-looking seventy-five-year-old with a blond bob and a dark jacket and slacks, approached the globe, accepted a Sharpie, and said, “Right under my very good friend and shipmate Don Walsh.” People craned their necks. A partygoer whispered, “Where do you sign the globe if you’re an astronaut?”
Afterward, Sullivan retired to the terrace. Deep-sea exploration, she said, “is not a bad analogue for going into space.” Both require a vehicle “that can take your squishy little body to a place that it clearly doesn’t belong. I’m comfortable inside, and I look through a window and know that right out there I would die. How is it possible for me to be here, eating my tuna-fish sandwich?” She went to Challenger Deep, the bottom of the trench, in 2020. “The word that kept coming to mind was ‘moonscape,’ ” she said. “A fine, silty sediment, gently rolling bottom, a little more tan than the gray of the moon”; barren, to our eyes, with “typically unsexy critters like burrowing worms.” As for space, “It’s a very dramatic experience, getting off the planet,” she said. “You’re basically riding a bomb for eight and a half minutes. And then you have the magical experience of being effectively weightless, maneuvering and living and working in zero gravity, which is great, great, great fun. And the view is stupendous.” Her crews’ data collection would seem tedious to outside observers, she said, but on one mission, “we deployed the Hubble Space Telescope.” Many of the people whose signatures appear on the globe had been meaningful to her (Earhart, Walsh, Armstrong, “the whole Apollo 8 crew”); as a kid, she’d admired astronauts and Jacques Cousteau. “These were people living inquisitive and adventurous lives,” she said. “I wanted my life to be like that.” ♦

articles.title_orig: Top oil executives dropped from event schedule after Riyadh attacks
articles.title_zh: Top oil executives dropped from event schedule after Riyadh attacks
articles.content_orig:
As Saudi Arabia reckons with the deadliest attack on its soil in more than a decade, questions swirl over how Riyadh will respond as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis continue to wreak havoc on the kingdom.
The kingdom launched a major offensive last week to support Yemeni government forces fighting the Houthis, but the rebels have so far held their ground.
Instead, they have escalated their campaign against the kingdom, culminating in missile attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport over the weekend that killed at least 13 people.
Drawing from Iran’s playbook in its conflict with the United States, the Houthis are vowing a painful escalation, targeting critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and imposing a global economic cost.
The Houthis have longstanding grievances against Saudi Arabia over Riyadh’s decade-long war against the group, which triggered the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. The recent Houthi escalation, however, is increasingly seen as an extension of Iran’s conflict with Washington.
After eleven years of trying to contain the Houthi advance militarily and through talks, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and his brother, Defense Minister Khaled bin Salman, face limited options. Across the border, the rebels have grown more powerful, consolidating control over major cities and pushing to seize others, such as the densely populated Taiz.
“This threat has to be dealt with once and for all,” Ali Shihabi, an author and commentator on Saudi politics told CNN. “A lot will depend on the performance of the Yemeni government troops on the ground and Saudi is helping them extensively with air power.”
So far , Saudi Arabia has largely confined its role to providing air cover for the anti-Houthi Yemeni coalition, stopping short of any major deployment of its own troops on the ground. Whether that restraint will hold after Saturday’s strike on Riyadh remains an open question.
Sending large numbers of Saudi troops into Yemen would plunge the kingdom into a an expensive and grinding ground war across rugged terrain and undercut the image Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is carefully cultivating of a stable, investment-friendly kingdom and global tourism hub.
Barely two decades ago, the Houthis were little more than a small religious revivalist movement. With Iranian backing, they have since grown into a formidable fighting force in possession of ballistic missiles and capable of striking as far away as Tel Aviv.
“They’ve developed their warfare,” a southern Yemeni official who fought the Houthis for years told CNN. “They’ve gotten more sophisticated in their attacks, they’re persistent and they’ve enhanced their intelligence.”
Yemen’s government alleges that Houthi rebels have worked with Iranian Revolutionary Guard experts to modify missiles into more effective weapons.
The new missiles fly faster and use a thermal-tracking system to home in on any heat source, Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemen’s armed forces, said. It remains unclear whether such missiles were used during Saturday’s attack on Riyadh airport.
The Houthis’ pursuit of more sophisticated weapons may now be extending into artificial intelligence.
AI company Anthropic said a group based in northern Yemen used its Claude AI tools to help develop guidance software for rockets and missiles – the systems that steer and stabilize the weapons in flight. The report did not identify those involved, but their location in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen suggests a possible link to the rebels.
Saudi Arabia has sought support from partners across the world to counter the group. France, Britain and Pakistan have committed support, while other allies like Turkey are considering sending help.
Prince Mohammed has also reportedly turned to Syria for help. Its president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, had led armed factions that successfully drove Iranian-backed groups from Syria after nearly a decade of civil war.
Yet Riyadh’s biggest ally, the US, has not supported air strikes on the Houthis, instead sending more than 100 military advisers to provide intelligence under a newly formed joint command.
Last year Washington reached a ceasefire with the Iran-backed group that reopened the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the maritime chokepoint through which global trade flows between Asia and Europe, to US vessels. Prince Mohammed spoke twice with Trump last month , urging him to strike the Houthis, sources told CNN at the time, but the president declined to intervene.
How a series of miscalculations restarted Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen
“Clearly, direct US involvement via air power would help because US aircraft can respond to US satellite intelligence more rapidly,” Shihabi said. “Saudi aircraft… are one stop removed from that loop so US involvement would be helpful.”
Saudi Arabia, one of the largest countries in the Middle East, remains vulnerable despite procuring some of the most advanced US air defenses. Its infrastructure, which carries rich resources across vast desert terrain, leaves it an easy target for the cheaper one-way drones developed by the Houthis.
Among those killed in the Houthi attack on the Riyadh airport was an American citizen, the Saudi civil aviation body said Sunday – an attack that might draw Trump further into the war.
“The Saudis are good fighters,” Trump told reporters following the attack. “But I think the attack was a terrible thing.”
Asked whether the US will join strikes on the Houthis, the US president said: “We may”

articles.title_orig: A Swiss retired pastor witnesses the life reality in Lebanon
articles.title_zh: A Swiss retired pastor witnesses the life reality in Lebanon
articles.content_orig:
Rev. Serge Fornerod brings forty years of international experience in development, public administration and ecumenical relations. Following the fall of the Berlin Wall, he managed aid and development programmes in Eastern Europe and later contributed to international relations within the umbrella organisation for Switzerland’s Protestant Churches. Since retiring in 2023, he has remained active in ecumenical networks, supporting the Foundation for Aid to Reformed Protestantism and the John Knox International Reformed Centre in Geneva.
Rev. Fornerod is a former member of the World Council of Churches central committee. He is also involved in preparations for the 2027 Francophone Christian Forum and researches the spread of early Christianity, particularly in the East . He took time to reflect on a new blog he has created that documents his experience at the Near East School of Theology (NEST) in Beirut, and his thoughts on the key to Christian unity.
What inspired you to start your blog to document your experience at the Near East school of Theology in Beirut?
Rev. Fornerod: Through this blog, I ’ d like to share some reflections and convictions I have formed over the last few years within the ecumenical movement and in my personal life.
The first is that when a parent is unwell, seriously afflicted by illness for years on end, telling them – as I often read on social media from “ good Christians” and – sorry to say – even church leaders – “ we ’ re thinking of you” or “ our prayers are with you” only helps the person saying it. Potentially, such phrases eventually add to the parent ’ s suffering, leaving them feeling even more alone. Someone who is ill, someone in despair, someone rendered invisible and voiceless by misfortune and injustice – that is someone you visit. You must take the time to listen and truly understand what the other person is going through. I believe that the Christian West (in general) takes its responsibility towards situations of suffering in the world and the churches experiencing them far too lightly. If we truly believe that the faith and life of churches elsewhere in the world concern us directly, then we must talk less about “ solidarity” – when this has no impact on our daily lives – and take more action. "Witness is with-ness.”
The second message is that in the world of ecumenical relations or relations between churches, the key to unity is not primarily dialogue, but listening. In light of everything that has been happening in the Middle East for decades, but especially since October 2023, I wanted to come and listen to the voices of Christians on the ground. Back home in Switzerland – though I fear this may also be the case elsewhere – I had the impression that opinions were quickly set in stone regarding who the culprits and who the victims were. My limited experience of the Middle East so far has very quickly made me feel uncomfortable in the face of so many so-called certainties, which in fact conceal unacknowledged political and cultural preconceptions. I wanted to give more space to the concrete reality of people ’ s lives and the experiences of the churches here. To listen, one must step back from one ’ s own context; one must be prepared to remain silent for a long while; one must be prepared to place trust first and foremost in the person who is in that situation; and one must draw closer, physically as well. The NEST faculty, with its international and ecumenical identity—driven by young people and researchers rather than officials (whom I also meet frequently and with pleasure!)—strikes me as an ideal place for observation, networking, and gathering information.
What do you hope others gain from you sharing your learning pilgrimage?
Rev. Fornerod: I hope to raise awareness amongst as many readers as possible of the need to take the time to reflect and find out more before forming an opinion on what is happening in this region. But also to show that it is relatively easy to obtain insightful background information on people ’ s experiences and the living conditions under which people here must face these new challenges. Action is easily possible and effective. When you consult the local sources here, it is striking to see, for instance, how many people in Israel oppose the destruction campaign of the Israeli army and how many people in Lebanon are engaged in bringing help. And lastly to hear that, for the Christians here, there is quite simply no alternative but to hold their heads high and carry on fighting day in, day out for dignity and justice – whether in their personal lives, their country ’ s politics or international justice. And if there is a Westerner present at the gatherings where people pray for this here, then perhaps that might do a little good.
Can you describe the way in which you are engaging with people?
Rev. Fornerod: One of the very nice and positive aspects of “ just being here,” free enough to engage with people is indeed to see the ease, spontaneity, hospitality, and kindness with which the Lebanese respond to your presence, however surprised they might be. It is a life lesson to see that, in an international, national, economic, and social situation as complicated and desperate as the one here, people naturally manage to draw strength from and take pleasure in making you happy.

articles.title_orig: The World's Hottest AI Stock Market Has Gone Cold
articles.title_zh: The World's Hottest AI Stock Market Has Gone Cold
articles.content_orig:
South Korea's stock market has gone from the world's hottest to its coldest in just a few months.
The Kospi, the world's best-performing major stock benchmark in the first half of 2026, has since fallen about 24%, making it the worst-performing major market in the second half. It's still more than 50% higher this year.
The AI trade isn't losing its appeal. But investors are increasingly looking beyond South Korea's memory-chip giants to companies with broader exposure to the AI hardware boom.
In July, analysts at GlobalData.TS Lombard pointed out that much of the earnings growth at Korean memory-chip makers came from higher memory-chip prices. By contrast, TSMC and Japanese chip-equipment makers relied more on advanced manufacturing and process expertise, giving them more durable growth prospects, they added.
Taiwan's Taiex has climbed about 7% in the second half of the year, taking its year-to-date gains to about 70% as investors broaden their bets across the AI hardware supply chain.
South Korea's rally was driven largely by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, whose soaring memory-chip profits made them among the biggest winners of the AI boom. Together, the companies account for more than half of the Kospi, leaving the market unusually dependent on a single segment of the semiconductor industry.
Even blockbuster earnings are no longer enough to excite investors. Last Thursday, Samsung forecast a nearly ninefold increase in quarterly operating profit, yet its shares have fallen for two straight trading sessions.
The reversal followed months of extraordinary volatility. The Kospi plunged 22% in July, its worst month since the 2008 financial crisis, before rebounding 18% on the month's final trading day for its biggest one-day gain on record. The swings triggered multiple market-wide circuit breakers as leveraged bets on chip stocks amplified the moves.
Young South Koreans flooded social media with memes and dark humor about their battered portfolios, while regulators tightened rules on leveraged single-stock exchange-traded funds after concerns the products had fueled speculation.

Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Trading has cooled sharply. Turnover has dropped 70% from its late-May peak, while foreign investors have continued pulling money from Korean equities.
The shift didn't happen overnight.
Even before Korea's selloff, investors were debating whether the next phase of the AI boom would continue rewarding memory-chip makers or broaden to companies with exposure across the semiconductor supply chain.
Taiwan appears to be benefiting from that shift. Its market offers exposure across AI infrastructure, from advanced chip manufacturing and packaging to servers and networking equipment.
That includes TSMC as well as companies involved in advanced packaging, servers, networking equipment, and other AI infrastructure.
The Taiex outperformed the Kospi by more than 23 percentage points in the third quarter, as Taiwan's benchmark gained nearly 4% while South Korea's plunged more than 19%.

articles.title_orig: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’
articles.title_zh: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout.
International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down.
"People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future."
Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work.
What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said.
That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said.
The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces.
World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them.
The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away."
The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said.
Banga, however, is less pessimistic about the disruption to the job market from AI. "Large language models are estimated probably to create some degree of disruption in jobs in the developed world," he said. "But by the time you get to middle-income countries and lower-middle-income countries, actually, the opportunity from small AI to build jobs and build productivity is enormous," he told CNBC on Tuesday.
AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said.
"Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva.
Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it."
AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training.
